Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge; non-contradiction consists in the stability of purposeful action. Even in the case of words, there is non-contradiction because they communicate the speaker’s intention—that object which appears in the mind as the domain of the speaker’s activity.
In that case, the validity of the word is not based on the reality of the object;
because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, its status as a means of knowledge regarding conventional objects is not accepted,
since activity is primarily directed toward things to be abandoned or acquired.

And because there is a difference in the cognition's apprehension due to the difference in the form of the object, its existence [as valid] follows from that very [apprehension]; thus, the nature [of validity] is known by itself.
Validity is established through worldly practice; the treatise serves to remove delusion.
Alternatively, [valid cognition] is the illumination of an object not previously known; for, after the apprehension of its own nature,
there arises a cognition of a universal regarding a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that was previously unknown— this is the intended meaning when considering the particular characteristic.
In the same way, the Blessed One is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of turning away from what is unreal;
his speech regarding reality depends upon [the removal of] obstacles, and therefore his status as a means of valid cognition is logical.
There is no such thing as an eternally existing means of valid cognition, because validity consists in the correspondence with a real entity.

Because the object of knowledge is impermanent, that [cognition] lacks stability; because it arises sequentially, there is no production from a permanent [cause]; and because dependence [on conditions] is impossible, even if [the cause] were impermanent, it would not be a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇatā*), since it cannot be assisted in any way.
Whether [the argument concerns] persistence, activity, specific configuration, causal efficiency, and so forth,
there is either the proof of what is already accepted, or non-establishment in the example, or else doubt;
for [causal efficiency] is established as following upon the presence or absence of a controller.

That which is inferred from this [perception], such as the arrangement [of parts] and so forth, is appropriate only for a specific entity; however, an inference based on a non-differentiating commonality of words for a thing well-known to exist in distinct entities is not valid,
just as one cannot infer fire from a mere white substance.
Otherwise, because a potter produces some modification of clay such as a jar, it would follow that even an anthill is his work;
for when an effect is used as a probans, even in its general form, it must be accompanied by the property to be proven.
The fallacy known as *kāryasama* (balancing the effect) is considered to consist in stating a distinction based on a difference in the related entities.

It is not logical to establish [the presence of horns] in sound and so forth by means of the commonality of the word "cow," because they belong to a different genus; it would be like [inferring horns] from the word "cow" alone, as in the case of [the fallacy of] "having horns."

Because they are dependent upon the speaker's intention, words do not exist anywhere [independently]. If, however, the existence of an object were established by the mere presence of those words, then everything would be established for everyone.
By this, the [arguments regarding] insentience and so forth concerning the followers of Kapila and others have been examined.
And consciousness [belongs] to that which is impermanent and so forth, because it [is observed] upon the removal of the skin at death.
This logical principle applies when the nature of the entity is unestablished; once established, the qualification is not a subverter.
Even if [the entity] is unestablished, it is not a subverter, just as sound has space as its locus.
Even when the word itself is unestablished, it establishes the established entity,
just as the proof for corporeality and so forth was stated by the Buddhist against the Aulūkya;
for even when there is deviation and so on regarding that [entity], the word remains non-deviant.
A proof possessing defects should be understood as such because the real thing is established by way of its reality.
Just as that thing is a cause, so too is it a non-cause.
When it is a cause, for what reason is it not accepted as a non-cause?

Just as Caitra’s wound-healing [is not attributed] to a tree stump that is unrelated to his connection with the medicine prescribed in the medical treatise, why is causality not likewise imagined for an unrelated stump? Furthermore,
without a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even an operation (*vyāpāra*) is not tenable.

Because that which is eternal lacks exclusion [from its effect], its causal capacity is difficult to establish. If one imagines another cause for those conditions in the presence of which an effect necessarily occurs, there would be an infinite regress of causes everywhere.

The earth and other elements are the cause for the production of a sprout through their transformation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-pariṇāma*), because a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) is observed in them when they have been prepared; just as the conjunction of object and sense-faculty [produces cognition] without [any further] specific quality.
If it is argued that this [collection] is likewise the cause of cognition, that is not so; for even in that case, there is no distinction [in their nature].

Since those things that are individually incapable would remain incapable even when combined—provided there is no excellence in their intrinsic nature—an excellence must therefore be established [as arising from their combination].

Therefore, those things which are individually incapable but in whose combination a quality is conceived possess causality through their union; this does not apply to [theories such as] God and the like, because there is no distinction [in their case].
Furthermore, validity consists in the knowledge of an imperceptible object and the means for its accomplishment.
Some declare that because [the self] does not exist, there is no practice;
for those who suspect deception in the instruction of one who is ignorant, some person possessing knowledge is sought in order to carry out what has been taught by him.
Therefore, let his knowledge regarding that which is to be practiced be investigated;
of what use to us is his thorough knowledge of the number of insects?
He is the knower of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and of the means for their abandonment and attainment.
He who is accepted as a valid authority (*pramāṇa*) is not one who knows everything;
whether he sees far or not, he must see the truth that is intended.
If it were the case that one who sees far is the authority, then come, let us worship vultures!

The means of accomplishment [of omniscience] is through the cultivation of compassion; however, since that intellect depends upon the body, if it is argued that cultivation is impossible, we say no, because the dependence [on the body] is refuted.
For the vital breaths, the exhalations and inhalations, the sense organs, and the intellect do not arise from the body alone.

Because there would be the over-extension [of the argument] that things independent of their own kind could take birth upon birth, [one must ask]: what was present in that which is seen to possess the capacity for reconnection,
such that it later lacked it and thus failed to reconnect?
There is not a single part of the earth or other elements where beings such as those born from moisture do not arise; therefore, everything has the nature of a seed.
This is because [the production] of the sense organs and so forth occurs without depending on their own specific species.
If transformation were [the case], it would apply to one and all without distinction;
even when each of the sense organs is impaired, there is no impairment of the mind according to your view, yet when this [mind] is destroyed, their destruction is also observed.

Therefore, that which is the support for the persistence of cognition, being itself dependent upon cognition, is the cause of the sense organs; hence, the sense organs [derive their function] from cognition. Whatever kind of projective force that [cognition] possessed previously, let it remain of that same kind afterwards as well.

Because it is assisted by the cognitions of those [senses], the mind is said to be dependent on the body. Although cognition does not occur without the sense organs, nor do they occur without it, nevertheless, because they are mutual causes, they are therefore mutually caused.
A successive entity does not arise from that which is non-successive, nor does it arise from dependence on something that lacks distinction.
Since cognition arises successively from the body, this indicates that the body itself must also possess succession.
For at every moment, each preceding moment would be the cause of the subsequent one.
Since its cause is therefore seen to exist at all times,
what contradiction is there in the final consciousness connecting with another mind? Likewise, why is it thought that the mind does not connect [with another] due to external objects?
If the object is not established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), why is the tenet (siddhānta) followed?
If it is because of a deficiency in the reason (hetu), then why was that very [deficiency] not stated here?
Since its apprehension occurs like the cognition of that [object], mental consciousness (mano-jñāna) does not arise from the sense-faculty (indriya).
Because there is a distinction in the capacity to produce cognition, it does not [arise] from the whole either;
nor from anything else, because that would lack consciousness and because there is no difference in the cause.
Coexistence [is impossible], as in the case of the sense organs, or like color and taste, since modification occurs through the medium of the object.
That which constantly assists an entity by being invariably concomitant with it is its cause; therefore, the locative case is used [in the expression] "from arising" (*utpādāt*).
Or, let there be something that occasionally assists the mental continuum.
The cessation of jars and other objects does not occur merely by that [reasoning], like that of fire and so forth;
furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the mind not ceasing while it remains in the body.
Since the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) exist when that [mind] exists and are subject to its control, the [mind] is therefore not those two.

How could there be impelling and attracting of the wind without effort? There would be the occurrence of decrease and increase [in those movements] due to the decrease and increase of those two [efforts]. This same consequence applies equally to those two [impelling and attracting], but it is not equal in the case of the cause of the mind.
Furthermore, another cause is required for the maintenance [of the body] by means of an infusion;
if it were argued that the body is not rendered defective by the humors (*doṣa*)— just as a wick and so forth [are not defective by their fuel]—
then there would be a return to life once the humors have been pacified after death.
If it is argued that [the defect] does not cease because, even when the fire has been extinguished, the transformation of the wood does not cease—[we reply:
no, because of the application of medical treatment;
for in some cases, a certain transformation is produced such that there is no recurrence.
In some cases, it may be reversed, as fire is [removed] from wood or gold;
yet even if another [impurity] is initially present and cannot be removed, that which is produced can be brought back,
for its transformation would be a return to its original state, like the hardness in gold.

Because a healer is difficult to find, some diseases are said to be incurable; or, [they are incurable] due to the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyuḥ-kṣaya*). However, when there is only a disorder (*doṣa*) [without these other factors], there is no incurability.
Even after death, [the patient may revive] through the neutralization of poison and the like, or by cutting off the bite.
When the cause of modification has ceased, it does not even breathe; how much less could there be a transformation of the derived effect when its material cause remains unmodified?
Just as a pot or similar object cannot be produced from clay if the clay itself remains unmodified.
For when one object is modified without having first modified another entity,
that [latter] cannot logically be its material cause (*upādāna*), just as a cow is not the material cause of a gavaya.
This is likewise the case for the mind and the body, because the arising of the effect is caused by that [body].
Co-existence arises from cooperation, like the case of fire and the melting of copper.
Since neither the existent nor the non-existent can lack a substratum, a substratum is not the cause of stability.
If it were the substratum of an existent, it would not be distinct from that which abides.
Even if there is a distinction [between the cause of destruction and the entity], that [cause] is the cause of that [destruction]; what has been done to the entity by it?
If you think that the consequence of non-destruction [of the entity] follows [from this], then that same consequence applies there as well; so what further use is there for a cause of persistence?

If it is argued that its persistence results from the arrival of non-destruction, then this is simply the nature of things regarding destruction; since this [destruction] is a real sublation, what is the use of a cause for its persistence?
If it is claimed that water and the like require a support, the same applies here as well.

For since entities perish at every moment, it is because the continuum of those entities arises in such a way that it possesses a cause; otherwise, a substratum would be untenable. [In the case of] water and so forth, there is a substratum because of the obstruction of their movement.
What need have qualities (*guṇa*), universals (*sāmānya*), and motions (*karman*)—which are themselves devoid of motion—for substrata?
By this, the inherence (*samavāya*) and the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) are also refuted;
for the fixed distribution of universals and so forth is denied, as they lack any support.
If its destruction occurs due to something else, what is the use of a cause for its duration?
It would perish even without other factors; causes for duration have no power [to prevent it]. Everything that has duration has a support, and everything that arises has a support.
Therefore, no entity whatsoever ever undergoes destruction. If its nature is inherently perishable, what other agent could establish it?
If its nature is not inherently perishable, what other agent could establish it?
Even the decrease and increase of wisdom and other qualities occur through the differentiation of mental activity, without any decrease or increase in the body;
this [phenomenon] is not found among things that depend on a substrate, such as the light of a lamp.
Even from that, there would be no distinction for this [mind] if the mind were not being assisted;
for the increase of passion and so forth arises at times from the nourishment [of the body] and the like, which are born of pleasure and pain,
and these two arise from the proximity of internal objects such as the equilibrium of the bodily elements (*dhātu*).

By this, the loss of memory and other such effects arising from the conjunction [of various factors] are explained. It is cognition alone, born from a specific internal object, that causes transformation in certain instances where there is an excellence in the mental continuum, as in the case of tiger's blood and the like.
Just as delusion and the like arise from hearing and seeing,
therefore one's own latent impression (saṃskāra) follows it with necessity;
just as the impression of what was heard and so forth is produced in every mind.

Because it is manifested in time and is non-different [from the self], the quality [of consciousness] would likewise exist even in the body. For one who possesses attachment to the self and seeks the avoidance of suffering and the attainment of pleasure, there is the assumption of a low state [of rebirth], which cannot be brought about by any other sentient being.
Deluded cognition regarding suffering and craving are the causes of bondage for living beings; he in whom these two do not exist does not undergo birth.
If it is argued that coming and going are not perceived because the sense faculties are unrefined, [the answer follows].
Just as the subtle smoke arising from a fire is not seen by one with weak vision,
so too some material entity, due to its subtlety, lacks the capacity to be perceived in certain cases—
like water in a spring or gold in ore— not because it is non-existent.

If the hand and so forth were to tremble, it would follow that everything [to which they belong] must also tremble; for it is impossible for a single action to exist [in one part] while its opposite exists [in another]. Otherwise, there would be a separate establishment [of parts].
Furthermore, when one [part] is covered, everything would be covered; and when one is not covered, [everything else] would likewise not be covered.
If one [atom] were colored, then color would be seen in that single [atom], or else there would be the perception of the uncolored;

therefore, there is no such thing as a single composite. Even if there were multiplicity, it would be as before: if you argue that motion is not established because there is no distinction [between atoms] and because they are atomic in size, that is not proven.
There is no distinction [in this regard] for those things that possess specific qualities; therefore, they are not atomic.
By this, the non-existence of obscuration and so forth is also refuted.
Or else, how could [the gold] mixed with dross and the like, or a heated stone and the like, [be perceived]?
If the object of perception is distinct [from the senses], how can there be cognition for those [senses] such as the eye which are individually incapable?
If it is argued that [cognition occurs] through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then the same logical consequence applies here as in the case of gold and the flux.
If it is claimed that the conjunction is perceptible, then how can there be cognition when the substratum is unperceived?

Furthermore, the association of taste, color, and so forth [with a substance] is contradictory; if it is claimed [to be established] through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then let there be a distinction in cognition. But how could [such a thing apply to] a "long row" or the like?
In that same way, number, conjunction, action, and so forth would also [be mere designations] by their own nature.
Furthermore, a form does not appear in the cognition as distinct from its verbal expression (abhilāpa).
This is because in verbal cognition accompanied by conceptual construction (vikalpa), which follows after the differentiation of objects,
it is like [the cognition of] qualities and so forth when they are merely imagined, or like [the cognition of things] that have perished or are yet to be born.

If it is held that there is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) here, then why is that very basis upon which it depends not accepted as the cause for both [the cognition and the designation] in all things? If it is argued that the metaphorical designation does not apply everywhere because the qualifying attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*) are distinct, [then...]
If it is asked: "How can there be different referents for words that denote the same primary object? [The reply is:

Even when they do not have different objects as their causes, words such as "white" and so forth are non-synonymous with respect to those possessing number and other qualities; if, in that case as well, there were a different object [for each].

There would be no distinction between quality (*guṇa*) and substance (*dravya*), even though they are different due to their distinct exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Even if [the quality] were not a separate entity from the object, it would be like the words "non-action" (*akarma*) and "non-substance" (*adravya*). Furthermore, that which is indicated by words denoting an entity (*bhāva*) appears as if it were distinct [from the substance].

When words such as "number" and so forth denote both the quality and that which possesses it, the auditory perception (*śruti*)— for one desiring to know only that [quality]— does not exclude all other distinct properties;
rather, in certain cases, it expresses a distinct property, as in the expression "the joining of the fingers."
The term "fingers" (aṅguli) is a denoter of the substratum (dharmin) because it implies all [the fingers] through their conjunction;
likewise, even when expressing a single well-known object,
it functions without implying the distinct capacities for color and so forth, as its established status is fixed in that manner.

The word "jar" excludes what is not its cause while having a result identical to it; therefore, the expression "the jar is not color" is a co-referential usage. Such is this distinction between that which denotes a genus and that which denotes a collection.

When it is said that "color and so forth belong to the jar," those specific powers (śakti-bheda) are made known as being subordinate to their common substrate; other things to be expressed should also be understood by this same method.
Furthermore, when all [the causes] are present as the cause, [the effect does not arise] even if a single factor is deficient.
Even if each [cause] possesses the capacity [to produce the effect], there would be the simultaneous occurrence of many [effects],

because multiplicity is equal [in all cases]. Nor can inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) be the restrictors [of the production of a single effect], for even if [the self] were one, there would still be multiple manifestations, since their cause is eternally present.
If it is argued that [the mind] does not have multiple causes, we say no, because there is no distinction;
for even in a single moment of life, multiple objects are apprehended simultaneously, and thus there is no restriction [on the number of causes].
Let it be that by a single cognition, multiple cognitions occur all at once.
Because there is no contradiction, let it not be that [the mind arises] even sequentially, since there would be no distinction [between the moments].
If many momentary vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of a different kind from itself are indeed postulated as the cause of such minds, [then this objection does not apply].
How could they possess succession without a cause that possesses succession?
If their own preceding members of the same class were the cause, the first one could not possibly exist;
for there is no such cause for it, or if there were, there would certainly be a multiplicity [of causes].

Because the vital breaths occupy different locations, cognitions therefore arise simultaneously. If multiple [breaths] occurring at the same time are the cause of a single consciousness, then that consciousness would not occur even when one [breath] is deficient, as in cases such as shallow breathing.

Now, if the cause exists according to its actual state, there would likewise be a distinction in the cognitions; for that [cognition] cannot be the effect of that [cause] if it does not differ according to the differences of the latter. Consciousness is the single cause of a single [effect] due to the restriction of its capacity.
02112 Because when cognition is impaired by attachment to another object, there is no apprehension of a different object;
02113 cognition, having arisen once from the body, is restricted by its own kind.
If it were dependent on something else, why would there be a cessation of the capable body?
If it is argued that once the body has ceased, the mind might remain in isolation without a support,
[we reply: if the continuum of consciousness does not serve as an auxiliary factor for obtaining the activity of its own cause, then it cannot persist.

The cause for the arising of another body is the five sense bases belonging to this life. Regarding the negation of their being causes for that [new body], non-perception is said to be non-conclusive; the same applies to the sense organs and so forth, as they are also "residual" (śeṣavat).

The capacity of the preceding sense organs is observed within their own respective species, as is established by the observation of their transformation; furthermore, their successive rebirth is proven. If that birth were from the body, then the same consequence as previously mentioned would follow.
If it is argued that the birth of another body arises from the mind itself,
then there is no such non-connection (asandhi) for all final moments of consciousness due to a deficiency of causes; therefore, this proof is considered to be *śeṣavat* (analogical).
If it is argued that even with practice, there should be no transcendence of one's inherent nature— just as in the cases of jumping, water, or heat— if that [nature] were indeed established,
it would require further effort; this would be the case only if its basis were unstable.

The particularity would not increase at all, nor would its intrinsic nature be of such a kind; for in that case, the means of proof, whose capacities have already been exhausted with respect to the subsequent particulars, would lack efficacy, and because it would eternally remain without a substratum.

Since a particular quality (viśeṣa) lacks intrinsic nature (asvabhāvatva), even when it has been produced during the process of intensification, it would not require further effort; otherwise, a different effort would be required to produce that particular quality, just as in the case of wood, mercury, gold, and the like, through fire and so forth. This applies to the mind as well.
Compassion and the like, born of practice, proceed by their own natural force;
therefore, once they have arisen, that becomes their innate nature and a quality. Subsequent effort serves only to produce further excellence within it.
And because the cognitions of compassion and so forth increase from seeds of a similar kind that preceded them, how could they remain stable even when practiced?
Nor is it the case that jumping arises solely from jumping, as it depends upon both strength and effort.
Because the capacity of its causes remains constant, jumping possesses a stable nature;
at first, due to a deficiency in the body, one cannot jump as before,
but once that deficiency is gradually removed through effort, one's own strength is restored.

Compassion arises from its own seed; if it is not obstructed by opposing factors arising from their own seeds, it reaches the state of being one's very nature. For thus, each preceding practice is the root of the subsequent one.
When the mental qualities such as compassion, dispassion, and awakening reach proficiency,
the nature of compassion arises through practice, just like [the mastery of] aversion, dispassion, and passion; thus,
for one who has perfected the excellence of compassion, there is the endurance of the suffering of others.
The compassionate one applies himself to the means for the sake of abandoning suffering;
for it is difficult to explain that goal and its cause when they are beyond direct perception.
Examining through both reasoning and scripture, he investigates the cause of suffering.
And because one perceives that there is no cessation of suffering while its cause remains in such a state— by means of the qualifiers of suffering itself, such as its impermanence and so forth—
one examines its opposite in order to abandon that cause of the result.
Its opposite is also established through the understanding of the nature of the cause:
attachment, which has conditioned phenomena as its object, is produced by the grasping at "self" and "mine.
The vision of selflessness is the opposing cause that subverts it.
Through many repetitions in various ways, by means of this method over a long period of time,
as one practices therein, virtues and faults become manifest;
and due to the sharpness of the intellect and the cause [of practice], the latent predispositions are abandoned.

This distinction of the Great Sage’s sword and other implements from ordinary objects consists precisely in the practice of skillful means; because they are for that purpose, they are considered "teachings" (śāsana).
Since these two exist prior to the accomplishment [of the goal], they are called "causes."
The abandonment of the cause possesses three qualities: the state of being a Sugata, due to non-reliance;
the teaching of suffering, due to the view of selflessness; and [the absence of] recurrence, which is stated to arise from birth and defects, or rather, through reasoning.

02141 Through the abandonment of the seed of the view of self, there is no returning; because of the nature of being distinct from that which has become [the self], there is the complete absence of afflictions and exhaustion. 02142 There is also no deficiency in body, speech, or intellect, nor any lack of proficiency in explaining the path.

Some say that there is no complete abandonment [of faults] through practice, because the destruction of defects such as verbal expression and the like is not certain; for this reason, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of this [practice] is doubtful and non-deviant. Furthermore, the defects are inexhaustible because they are eternal and there is no means [to destroy them].
Or one might imagine [the following]: "Because of the lack of thorough knowledge of the means.
[This is not so,] because of the possession of a cause; for through the repeated practice of the contrary cause, its destruction occurs.
By means of the knowledge of the nature of the cause, that knowledge [of the means] is also established.
The Tāyin (the Protector) teaches the path he has himself perceived; because his teaching would otherwise be fruitless, he does not speak untruth.

This is due to his compassion and because all his undertakings are devoted to the welfare of others. Therefore, either the Tāyin is authoritative, or else the revelation of the Four Noble Truths is authoritative.
The aggregates of one in saṃsāra are suffering, because passion and the like are observed to be intense;

because they arise from habituation and not by chance; and because birth would be impossible if there were no cause. Furthermore, it is not the property of wind and so forth, because of the confusion of their natures and because of deviation.
If it is argued that there is no fault [in this], why is another property of that [object] not also perceived?
It is not the case that all properties are perceived by everyone, because that would entail the consequence of everyone having the same degree of passion.
If it is argued that there is no fault because it is like color and so forth, then the same objection applies to that as well.
If there were no predominance of specific karmas in that regard,

then even when there is a distinction [in the results], it would be unestablished because the defects [of the causes] remain undifferentiated. Furthermore, a modification does not arise from a modification, nor are all [modifications] produced by everything.
Furthermore, it is not logical for the effect to diminish while the cause is increasing.
Just as in the case of heat and so forth, even the transformation of passion and the like arises from pleasure and so forth;
if it is argued that passion does not arise because of pain produced by disharmony, [the response follows].
By what could it be said that intoxication arises from equilibrium? For passion increases from that [intoxication], and from that [passion] comes the god of love (*smara*).
Furthermore, one who is impassioned is seen even when the humors (*doṣa*) are in disequilibrium, while another is not seen to be so even when they are in equilibrium.
Moreover, others [experience intoxication] due to the depletion [of fluids] or the flow of blood; intoxication is not restricted to a single woman alone.
If it is argued that [the cognition] would not be intense with respect to even a single limb, form, and so forth, we say no;
for this is not the case for all [cognitions], as they are not non-conclusive (anekānta), nor would it be indeterminate.
Even for one who perceives only faults, there might be an apprehension of a limb as a quality.
If one were to perceive all qualities [of an object] due to the lack of distinction in the cause,
then a person who is considered to be full of passion in a certain state would likewise not be subject to hatred;
for since those two states are not dissimilar in form, no restrictive rule can be observed here.
For one whose [mental] states such as attachment and so forth function in dependence upon the specific latencies of their own kind, these faults do not follow as consequences;
by this, the status of being a property of the material elements and that of having a support are refuted.
Because of this negation, white and other such qualities do not reside in earth and the like;

furthermore, the term "derived from that" (tad-upādāya) signifies the logical reason (hetu), and [the qualities] are the substrata because they exist inseparably from their own basis— otherwise, it would be untenable.

If it is argued that there is no separation [of the power] from the entity, as in the case of the power of intoxication and so forth: [we reply] the power is not a distinct entity; for if it were, the entity would perish when the power departs from its substratum. If it is claimed that the power remains in the intact substratum and then departs, we say no, because of the distinction between them.
Because there is a perception of distinct appearances between the physical element and consciousness,
and because the mind would remain identical in form even when the body undergoes transformation,
what dependence on an external object could conceptual thought have, any more than it does with respect to visible forms and the like?
When, independent of the body, consciousness arises for someone as the cause of awakening to latent impressions (vāsanā),
then by that [consciousness], something [else] may arise at some time;
and because there is no appropriation of consciousness by that which is non-conscious, [the existence of consciousness] is established.
If it is claimed that every entity is desired [to exist] because of its connection with the power of consciousness (*vijñāna-śakti*),
who else but this beast of a Sāṃkhya would venture to speak so shamelessly?
To say that "there are a hundred elephants on the tip of a blade of grass" when they have never been seen before!
That form which has come to be visible was not visible previously.

Even if the cause were dispersed in a hundred ways, how could that [form] exist? Furthermore, if there were the manifestation of something unprecedented, it would follow that there is no restriction regarding passion and so forth.

If everyone possessed passion and so forth because they do not transcend the nature of the elements (*bhūta*), then everyone would have identical passion; this is not the case due to the excellence of the elements.
Even though there is no difference in the vitality of the elements, this difference [in passion] has its basis elsewhere.
Because they possess decrease and increase, one should eliminate those [defilements] through their absence;
for if, despite the difference [in the substratum], there were no exhaustion of the nature that is the common cause of passion and so forth,
then passion would be identical everywhere, since its cause possesses an identical nature.
For there is nowhere any gradation in the cognition of "cow" arising from the same object—
whether in the case of earth and so forth, or here in the case of "livingness" and so forth;
nor is fire ever non-hot, even though there may be a gradation in its heat.
If it is argued that it is the same here as well, we say no; because there is no denial of the difference between fire and its heat.

For those qualities which belong to some other existing thing that is experienced in varying degrees are sometimes obstructed when there is a difference in that [substratum], just like whiteness and so forth.

There is no fixed rule for them [the sense organs], as there is for color-form and so forth, because they are not distinct from the primary elements (*bhūta*). If it is argued that this is the same [for the objects], it is not so, because it would follow that desire and the like would arise simultaneously [with their objects].
Furthermore, because they are objects of conceptual construction, external objects are not determinants [of specific cognitions].

Due to the absence of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), there would be no restriction regarding passion and the like, or else all cognitions would arise at all times because their causes are ever-present. Since they are perceived only occasionally, they are impermanent; moreover, because they rely upon defects, they are not eternal.
Suffering exists because it is subject to causes; it is neither the self nor presided over by one.
There is no causeless presider, nor can that which is eternal be a producer. Therefore, the manifold does not arise from a single [cause] at a different time.

Because an effect is not produced even when other causes are assembled, there would be an inference of another cause; this [inference] does not apply to eternal things. By virtue of its occasional occurrence, the fact that this suffering has a cause is established.
"Either there is eternal existence or eternal non-existence for that which is causeless, because it does not depend on anything else;
just as there is no cause for the sharpness and so forth found in thorns and the like,
so too this [world] would be without a cause— thus some declare."

That in the existence of which there is birth, or in the modification of which there is modification, they call that its cause; and that [cause] exists for them as well. Because touch is the cause of form, it possesses the status of a causal condition in the act of seeing.

By the refutation of eternal [entities], the existence of a Creator God and the like is also precluded; because of their lack of capacity, the cause [of rebirth] is therefore the grasping of the desire for existence,
since it is produced by the human hope for the attainment of a particular place.

That desire for existence is the activity toward pleasure and pain of one who desires acquisition and non-acquisition; furthermore, since both the desire for objects of sense and the desire for power are held to belong to living beings,
it proceeds everywhere because self-love is its cause.
Because one perceives pleasure in what is not pleasure, craving is the basis for existence;
thus the Teachers proclaim that since birth is not seen in one who is dispassionate,
and since passion is not seen in one without a body, passion arises from the body.
Because one approaches the causal sign (*nimitta*), the [desire for] appropriation (*upādāna*) is accepted; however, [if one denies it], that which is desired is obstructed.
But one who desires this reasoning contradicts his own position by himself.
If [you argue that] there is coexistence with birth because passion is seen in those already born, [we reply:]...
The prior establishment of the homogeneous class (*sabhāga-jāti*) has not been stated even though it serves as a cause;

ignorance has been mentioned [as the primary factor], while craving alone is the driver of the continuum toward existence. Furthermore, karma is not the cause because of its immediate succession, since [rebirth] would be impossible even when that [karma] exists.
That [liberation] is not final because obstacles to the cause and so forth are possible.
There is no lack of liberation due to being a transmigrating being, for that is not desired and is not established.
As long as there is no loss of love for the self, one will continue to suffer.
Having taken up [the burden of] suffering for that long, he does not remain at ease;
even though there is no liberator, effort is exerted for the sake of removing false superimpositions.
This occurs through compassion or even through the force of past karma in those who have transcended passion regarding various states of existence.

Since it is accepted that there is no turning back once [the momentum] has been projected, there is no need for further action to project [it], because the auxiliary causes have perished for those who have transcended the thirst for existence. For one who is not opposed to the knowledge of suffering, [the mind] continues to flow by means of previous formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

The arising and production of the nature of things does not conform to the existence of a sentient being; passion for a phenomenon that lacks that nature arises from the superimposition of another self.
Compassion arises merely through contact with the continuum of suffering.
And delusion is the root of the defects, and that [delusion] occurs without the grasping at a self.

Therefore, since there is neither hatred nor defect regarding the primary cause, compassion is considered [to be free from defects]. There is no non-liberation when the prior latent impressions have perished, because of the absence of reconnection with another [existence].

Those whose formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) possess undiminished power remain free from affliction; because their compassion is mild, they do not exert great effort toward [the world's] preservation. However, those for whom compassion is great remain [in the world] even while dependent on others.

If, upon the disappearance of the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there were non-existence from the very beginning on the path, then because that innate [view] has not been abandoned, or if it were abandoned, how could there be existence? For one who thirsts, thinking, "May I be happy in existence, or may I not suffer."
That very cognition which is "I" is itself the innate perception of a self (*sattva*).
For no one feels affection for a self without perceiving it as "I.
Nor does one who desires happiness rush toward [an object] without love for the self.
Bondage is the causality of the arising of suffering; how could that belong to an eternal [self]?
Liberation is the causality of the non-arising of suffering; how could that belong to an eternal [self]?
That which is inexpressible as impermanent cannot be the cause of anything at all.
Furthermore, how could bondage and liberation not exist even for that which is inexpressible?
The wise declare that to be eternal whose intrinsic nature does not perish. Therefore, abandoning this shameful view, let it be called eternal.
It has been stated that through the cultivation of the path, the basis (the psycho-physical organism) undergoes transformation.
If it were argued that even when [the path] has become habitual, the state of being afflicted by defects remains, that is not so, because [the path] is not all-pervasive, just like the path itself.
Just as the apprehension of objects is the inherent property of consciousness, so too is that [transformation].
It is grasped as its producer by virtue of its existing nature;
this is its natural state. However, when it deviates due to some other cause, it becomes unstable and dependent upon a further cognition, like the perception of a snake [in a rope].
This mind is luminous by nature; the stains are adventitious.
Since they were incapable even before that [luminosity], where would there be power for them later in that which consists of it?
They are not able to grow at all, like fire on a wet ground.
Even if a thing is capable [of being sublated], because it possesses within itself the capacity for the arising of a sublater,

there can be no sublation of that which has the nature of a real entity free from affliction by contrary cognitions, even if those cognitions exert effort, due to their partiality toward their own side.
Because they have a single source in the grasping at a self and because they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship,
attachment and aversion do not mutually exclude one another even though they are distinct.
Since they are not in contradiction with delusion, there is no absolute suppression of the defects by means of friendliness and the like.

All impurities have that as their root, and that [root] is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Because it is the opposite of true knowledge (*vidyā*), because it is perceived as a mental factor (*caitta*), and because it is joined with false perception and ignorance, anything else [proposed as its cause] is illogical.
The contradiction here must be explained;
and because of that contradiction, the contradiction of the view of emptiness with all [alleged] faults is established.
It is not indestructible, because it is a property of sentient beings, and because it is unestablished, like form and so forth.
Even when there is a connection [with the remedy], because the counteragent involves both abandonment and re-emergence,
there is no further arising of the fault that opposes it, as in the case of hardness;
for that [hardness] is not subject to removal due to its being an inherent nature (*ātmatva*), and because [the fault] is not invariably [removed], as in the case of ashes.
He who perceives a self develops a constant attachment toward it, thinking "I am. Due to this attachment, he craves pleasures; craving causes him to overlook faults.
Seeing only virtues and being intensely desirous, he thinks "this is mine" and thus takes up the means to achieve them.
Therefore, as long as there is adherence to a self, so long is one in saṃsāra.
When there is a self, there is the notion of "other"; from the distinction between self and other arise attachment and aversion. Bound up with these two, all faults are produced.

One who necessarily feels affection for the self does not become dispassionate toward what belongs to it; and since the self is faultless, there is no cause for the cessation of that affection. If you argue that affection is faulty, then what follows from that? Why should it be abandoned?
When its object is not perceived as faulty, it is impossible to abandon that [object];
for the abandonment of desire, aversion, and so forth, which follow upon the perception of qualities and defects,
occurs through the non-perception of those two in the object, but not according to the same process as with external things.
For attachment does not arise from the quality of attachment itself, but rather from the perception of the quality of the object;
when that cause is unimpaired, by what could the effect be prevented? Or what fault has been observed in attachment, other than its being the basis of suffering?
Nevertheless, there is no dispassion toward these [objects] because of the perception of ownership, just as there is none toward the self;
for if the self is not the cause of suffering without them, then they too are of that same nature.
Thus, both are faultless, and consequently, there can be no dispassion toward either.
If, through the cultivation of the perception of suffering, one abandons this [body] like a limb bitten by a snake,
it is by abandoning the notion of "mine" regarding it; but there is no such abandonment in the opposite case,
for the sense organs and so forth are grasped as the basis for experience.
By whom could the notion of "mine" regarding these [limbs] be prevented? Whence, then, could there be detachment toward them?
For everyone, it is directly perceived that when hair and other parts fall away from the body, that feeling of disgust arises, while elsewhere there is a sense of longing.
For in that case, one's own cognition is produced by relations such as inherence (samavāya) and so forth;
yet even when that relation is not perceived in that very way, it is not lost,
since the state of being a causal factor (upakāritā) exists everywhere, even in the absence of inherence and the like.
If it is argued that self-awareness does not arise toward [the body] because it involves suffering—just as one does not feel attraction toward a finger [when it is pricked]—that is not so;
for that suffering is not absolute, being for the most part like food mixed with poison.
Through the attainment of distinguished pleasure, there arises a state of detachment toward that which is contrary to it.
One might renounce some pleasure out of a thirst for a superior happiness;

however, regarding selflessness, one proceeds according to what is obtained out of attachment to a self. It is observed that even among animals, there is a desire for a beautiful woman when she is not obtainable.

How can one who holds the self dear desire its destruction? How could such a person desire [the cessation of] love, which is the very substratum of all experience, activity, and qualities? For the nature of love is not such [as that].
In every way, the grasping at a self firmly establishes attachment to the self;
that seed of attachment to what belongs to the self remains in its very state even when,
through the application of effort based on even a slight trace of virtue, one attains detachment from what belongs to the self.

One who possesses [right] conduct obstructs those faults and covers them over. If there were detachment even toward the self, then that which is currently detached would abandon the self; therefore, the meditation on suffering is useless.
Even by means of the cultivation of suffering, one would only perceive suffering;
for even though that was previously perceived directly, one was nonetheless not free from passion,
even if the mind wavered for a moment due to a fault in a single instance.
Even in that state of detachment, there is no lack of passion, just as a lover feels toward another woman;

for the attachment that arises toward a single object amidst the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted is the seed from which all subsequent attachments emerge in turn.

Affection has as its object that which is faultless, and the means [of achieving it] are likewise faultless. Since this entire world consists of nothing but this, where could he now become dispassionate?
Even if there were faults in those [objects], those same faults would equally apply to the self.
In that case, how could one who is not yet dispassionate toward those [objects] become dispassionate toward their defects?
For the perception of defects can only sublate the affection born from the perception of qualities;
yet such [dispassion] does not occur regarding the sense organs and so forth, since it is observed even in children and the like.
Because it exists even where there are defects, and because it exists by its very nature even where there are qualities;
or because the sense of "mine" is absent in things such as the past;
for that very reason, there is no perception of qualities in the notion of "mine" either.
For that [cause] is abandoned; therefore, it is not because of seeing a lack of virtue. Moreover, the attribution of non-existent virtues is indeed seen there due to affection.
Therefore, how can that injunction, which is the sublater of those causes, be sublated by it?
Because of the cognition of destruction and arising, there is the desire for what is superior and inferior;
therefore, people perceive the self as distinct from the sense faculties and so forth.
Consequently, even through the view of oneness, one does not feel affection [for others], since that person is attached to the self.
One is naturally attached to the internal objects of perception; however,
that revulsion toward present sufferings which is like hatred is not true dispassion, because even then one seeks another state [of existence].

Because hatred is the source of suffering, it persists only for that long; once it has ceased, it returns once more to its own original nature. But indifference toward everything arises from the abandonment of both rejection and appropriation.
That which is called dispassion belongs to those who are like the axe and the sandalwood;
having realized the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), the meditation on suffering was taught.
And that [meditation] is the arising of our cognition, which is the basis for the vision of selflessness.
But the logical reason for the view of emptiness is that all other meditations have that as their purpose.
For this very reason, he taught suffering from impermanence, and selflessness from suffering. And one who is not dispassionate possesses craving and relies upon all undertakings.
One who is not liberated from afflictions and karma is such a person as is called a "wanderer in saṃsāra.
For one who does not even desire what belongs to himself, there is no enjoyer;
nor, at that time, is there a self for him, since activity and enjoyment are indeed the defining characteristics of it.
Therefore, O seekers of liberation, uproot the view of a self (sattvadṛṣṭi), which has its seeds of a similar kind in an beginningless continuum; for [otherwise],
you would fail to see the basis for the existence of the scripture.
One who asserts that liberation occurs through scripture alone does not provide full satisfaction;
for a ritual procedure, even when fully perfected with seeds and other materials, is not sufficient to prevent the birth of men,
since it would follow that liberation could also result from oil massages, fire-burns, and the like.
Previously, due to the teacher's lightness, the removal of sin was not performed later;
let there be no weightiness for this [sin], for sin has no substantial form (*amūrta*).
This is due to the power of false cognition, the thirst arising from it, and volition.
Birth is the transition to an inferior state; therefore, when that [ignorance] is severed, birth does not occur.
For the causal capacity for birth resides in those two alone, since birth arises from them alone. These two, being conscious, constitute action itself; thus, they form the complete cause of birth.
The cause of movement and cognition is dependence on something other than themselves; these [movements] arise from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

Because that unseen force ceases, there is no movement; yet that [movement] is not a mental formation (*saṃskāra*), because the capacity [for action] arises from the production of the instrument, following upon the presence and absence [of that capacity].
It is observed that these [functions] belong to the intellect (*buddhi*) and not to anything else; do they not exist?
Retention, impulsion, agitation, and restraint are under the control of consciousness (*cetanā*).
If that [consciousness] were incapable [of acting], these functions would not occur immediately after initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, because the intellect would then be absent, [the afflictions] would not exist; yet they are joined with the impurities.
If the intellect were incapable of them, they would remain powerless even while one is alive.
This is because there is a decrease and increase in the strength of the opposing side and its own side during their cultivation.
Defects, which proceed from their own seeds, are not prevented even in one who has been initiated;
because that which is eternal is independent, successive production is contradicted,
as is both action and non-action in the case of an entity whose nature remains identical.
If there were identity between cause and effect, then because of their distinctness [from a third entity],

the status of being an agent and an enjoyer would be lost, and causal efficacy would not be established; furthermore, such consequences as remembering what another has experienced or enjoying what another has produced would not be avoided.
Because there is no memory of anything [without prior experience], for memory arises from what has been experienced;
thus, by superimposing sixteen unreal aspects upon the Four Noble Truths— such as "it is stable," "it is pleasure," and "I am"— one becomes intensely craving.
In that very state, right view, when well-cultivated, destroys the accompanying craving by conforming to the nature of reality which is the opposite of that [craving]; thus,
there is no further arising from the three causes, even though karma and the body persist.
Because it is impossible for there to be no cause, just as a sprout cannot arise without a seed;
because there is no possibility of a counter-example where karma and the body are eliminated;
and because it is impossible [to eliminate them] while craving persists, since [the cycle] would arise again.
And if effort were for the sake of destroying both [afflictions and karma], then labor toward the destruction of karma would be useless.
Furthermore, because a variety of fruits is observed, a diversity of potencies is inferred for karmas;
therefore, their destruction cannot result from that [single form of] heat-induced affliction alone.
How could the fruit produced by that [action] be anything other than small and not of a different kind?
Even so, through the power of austerity (tapas), by means of the blending or the destruction of [karmic] potencies,
it might be entirely eliminated from some affliction without even a trace of suffering.
If that which is desired as distinct from affliction is austerity, and if that [austerity] is indeed affliction,
then because it is the fruit of karma, there is no confusion of powers and so forth;
for even in the destruction of incipient defects and the like, [it acts] through opposition to the defects.
They would be capable of performing that very action; how then could there be a loss of what has been done?
Faults do not belong to the action itself; one does not act wrongly because of a fault, nor does desire for even happiness arise without false conceptualization.
Because it protects, it is the means for attaining stable and complete knowledge of reality;
because the root *gam* has the sense of "understanding," it is superior to external [teachings] and to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Therefore, its application toward the knowledge of the welfare of others is its compassion, and that is its teaching.

Therefore, because he does not cease from his commitment to the welfare of others once his own goal is accomplished, out of compassion he teaches what is beneficial— truth together with its means— based on his knowledge. And since he is diligent in speaking that [truth], he possesses the status of a valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
The praise of the teaching’s suchness is due to that very teaching;

for it is not excluded even from inference for the sake of establishing the reality of the means of valid cognition, or because one observes its application in the form: "Whatever has the nature of arising..."
"Everything has the nature of cessation," and so forth— in these and many other ways,
the mark (liṅga) which is the basis of inference is characterized by inseparable connection (avinābhāva).
And that [mark] is clearly stated as being the reason (hetu) through the demonstration of its pervasion (vyāpti) with the probandum (sādhya).
Cognition is of two kinds because the objects of cognition are of two kinds, based on their capacity or incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Hair-tufts and the like are not real objects because they lack the conviction that they are real objects;
furthermore, this is due to their being similar or dissimilar, and because they are either objects or non-objects [of valid cognition].
Because cognition arises from words even when other causes are present, [the object] exists or does not exist accordingly.
That which is capable of causal efficiency is here called ultimately real; everything else is declared to be conventionally real. These two are the particular and universal characteristics.
If it is argued that "everything is incapable," [we reply: the capacity of seeds and so forth toward sprouts and so forth is observed;
if you maintain that this [capacity] exists only conventionally, let it be so as it may.
If you claim that this [conventional capacity] exists everywhere, [we say no], because it is not established through the positive and negative concomitance of cognition.
Because the universal characteristic is not perceived, [the cognition of it is not produced], just like the cognitions of the eye, visible form, and so forth.

By this [same reasoning], the cognitions regarding the universal of "pot-lifting" and regarding number and so forth proceed in accordance with internal factors such as convention (*samaya*) and mental application (*ābhoga*).
Hair and the like are not universals because there is no conceptual adherence to them as objects;
since they are apprehended as objects of knowledge, the fault does not apply to non-existents.
Even if those [non-existents] were likewise [unreal], their clear appearance is not denied.
Because it is an object by virtue of having the nature of cognition, the notion that "it is hair and so forth" has as its object a universal;
for if [the appearance of] hair were an object by virtue of having the nature of cognition, it would follow that the universal is [the object].

Likewise, there is no fault because it is intended [as such]; there is equality by virtue of having the nature of the object, since it is of an identical form everywhere and because it relies upon the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from that. It is not a real entity because it is denotable; and it is purposeful because of the coordination of the sense-faculties.

When names and so forth are uttered, they are invariably connected to the speaker, the hearer, and the object denoted; therefore, there would be no application [of the word] toward an object that is unrelated to these. If it is argued that the application toward the object occurs through a delusion caused by similarity, then that application would not occur at all times.
And there is no delusion regarding location in cognition, because a cognition of such a kind arises [directly] from its own production;

for elsewhere, such a cognition is not admitted to exist there [in the external object]. Or, if it were to have the appearance of an external object, it would lack validity with respect to that means [of knowledge].
Because the exclusion [of an object] from consciousness is not established as being distinct [from it],
and because all cognitions have objects, yet in dreams and the like they are seen otherwise; therefore,
[the claim that objects exist only as mental constructs] is untenable, for blue and other such things appear as externalized impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Because it does not encounter resistance like blue and other objects, cognition is not [perceived] by those situated in a location suitable for it;
and because it is known by itself even while remaining unknown [to others], names and so forth have been described by this [same reasoning].
Why, then, is the cognition of the eye and other [senses] considered to possess the desired object?
If it is argued that [the word] is seen to have efficacy with respect to its object, then anything else would be rendered purposeless.
If it is claimed that there is no non-application [of the word] even when there is no connection [to the object], just as there is in the case of a connection with the object,
then the past and the future could not be denotable, because those [objects] have perished.
If it is argued that there is no such over-extension because the word apprehends the universal (*sāmānya*),
that is not so; for either the universal is not apprehended alone, or even if it is apprehended,
it is not distinct from that [particular], and thus [the universal] would be perceived eternally.
And because it is eternal, if the manifestation [of a universal] is for the sake of the perceptibility of the manifestation,
then that which is capable of producing cognition within itself is always capable;
or, if it is at some time incapable, then it is always incapable.
Whether it possesses power or lacks power, that which is established by its very nature cannot be remedied because of its permanence; who is capable of exhausting it?
Furthermore, that universal cognition is perceived as being continuous.
By whom was that slight trace of the form of blue and so forth produced within it?
If it is argued that the sense organs are not useless because they serve as the objects for perceptual cognition, [we ask]:
from what source does that cognition arise which has a distinct appearance from the single-natured sound and other [objects]?

The universal (jāti) does not exist as the form of the individual (vyakti) which possesses the universal, such that it would require another substratum. If it were established as distinct [from the individual], then its being an effect is indeed what is called "dependence.
Even though an effect is independent of anything else for its completion, it arises from its own cause.
How could that which is not an effect be connected with conceptual construction in any way?

If it were other [than the effect], it would be unconnected; therefore, its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established. There is no consequence of it being a universal (*jāti*) for a non-entity, because there is no dependence on those two due to their non-existence.
Therefore, although formless, it is conceptualized as the basis for forms;

it is manifested by words that intend to apprehend its specific distinctions. Whatever appearance of form occurs therein, or whatever apprehension of an object as a real entity takes place, [is merely a mental construction].
That error is produced by the habitual practice of perception since beginningless time. And as for that universal of objects which is characterized by the exclusion of others—
that upon which these words are based, it possesses no form whatsoever.
Because it is perceived even as a formless entity within the cognition of a universal,
that [cognition] should also be admitted to be an error regarding the object;
yet, because it lacks reality by way of having the form of an object, it is not possessed of form.

If it is held that [the ultimate] is inexpressible because of its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), yet is expressible in some way through verbal expression, then there is no such thing as the inexpressibility of things whatsoever. It is certainly not inexpressible, for due to the difference in the basis of designation (*upādāna-bheda*), there is a figurative application of difference.

Even regarding objects past and future, words function by being bound to universals (*sāmānya*); how then could there be a property (*dharma*) that is both existent and non-existent? If it is claimed that this [non-existence] is accepted through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then what [status] would belong to a present jar?

That proximity which does not exist between a cloth and its absence [is the basis for the cognition]; the unswerving operation of the intellect toward both the primary and the superimposed is always present,
just as there is a worldly convention regarding the lion and the boy.

Where a word is established by convention even for an unreal object, it is primary (mukhya) in that context; elsewhere, due to similarity with that, it is secondary (gauṇa), its application being faltering.
For example, the name "non-existence" is applied even where there is existence, or [the name of one thing is applied] according to a mere conceptual construction.
Whether one is incapable or capable, a person might formulate a scriptural statement concerning a primary cause and so forth;
yet, the kind of cognition that arises from words is seen to be exactly the same whether [the object] has perished or not—
this is not the case for the minds of the listeners and others regarding real objects.
Because both cognitions grasp only the universal, the universal belongs to both of them;
yet it has already been refuted that this [universal] can be grasped in isolation prior [to the particulars].
How could there be a non-distinct [universal] for things that are mutually distinct?
Or, if form possesses a dual nature, how could that entity be one?
It would have to be something other than those two if its form were identical to both;
thus there would be no relation between "those two," yet this is not a fault regarding their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

Therefore, in this case, the very state of being common is the characteristic of a non-entity (*avastu*) within that universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, it is held that such [a universal] would be manifold and perishable; because destruction is invariably concomitant with the existence of a real entity (*vastu*), it cannot be eternal.
Furthermore, universals lack a causal relationship [with particulars] because they are not effects, and thus they possess no form.
Moreover, that cognition which arises from the power of the real entity depends upon that [entity];
it does not depend on convention, and this is clearly perceived in the case of cognitions of universals.
Any cognition whatsoever that follows upon non-difference with respect to two objects at a single moment,
even without a linguistic convention, is based on the proximity of their objects;
for proximity among the eyes and other [senses] is accepted as existing even without a universal (jāti).
Whether it be a universal (*jāti*) that follows through various divisions in the effects of cognition,
it does not appear in any way whatsoever within consciousness, because its form is not manifested therein.
Even if there were a seer of the sense organs, that [universal's] body would have to appear [to him].
Because they possess form, universals are not perceived in their isolation;

furthermore, when an individual is perceived, that [universal] is not seen as anything other than the form of the word. Even if it were to perform the function of being a mere object of cognition, it would still be considered unfit for such a role.
Because it is incapable [of causal efficiency], that is formless; for that is the definition among non-entities.
That which is the opposite of what has been described is accepted as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
And that universal (*sāmānya*) is threefold, based on existence, non-existence, and both.
If cognition were dependent upon an existent entity because it follows from the existence of that entity,
[that is not so], because the answer has already been stated, and because [cognition] is observed in the case of the past and so forth otherwise.
If it is argued that [cognition] would lose its status as a property of an existent entity, [we reply that it does not], since it is preceded by the apprehension of the existent entity.
"Therefore, there is no fault in saying that [the result] is the cognition of that; however, the object of cognition (*meyam*) is only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Consequently, because existence and non-existence are investigated through the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and because that [particular characteristic] is apprehended both in its own form and in the form of others, two types of objects of cognition are accepted."
The second type of error is held to be that which occurs through an incorrect adherence [to an object].
If it were a cognition by way of another's form, it would not be an error; yet, because it is erroneous, it does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
However, even though it is erroneous, it possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge because it is non-deceptive with respect to its intended purpose.
Furthermore, movement is observed to be otherwise, and this position has already been refuted.
For one who runs toward both a jewel and the light of a lamp, thinking it to be a jewel,
although there is no difference in their false cognition, there is a distinction with respect to their causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
In whatever way [it may be], even though both inference and its fallacy lack correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatva*),

their status as valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is established by virtue of their conformity to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Wherever a cognition follows the presence and absence [of an object] through the causal efficacy of that object, [it is valid].
Therefore, its apprehension is independent; hence, another entity that is beyond the senses [is required].
Since its own nature is unperceived, if there were another thing based on an object which, being related through that basis, could serve as its indicator, then [it would be known].
At that time, the cognition occurs only by way of a general form that follows from the indicator;
therefore, no remote object is apprehended in its specific detail. And the cognition that arises regarding the subject (dharmin) from a property (dharma) related to it—
Inference is the sole means of establishing things that are beyond the reach of the senses;
there is no other object of cognition possible apart from the perceptible and the imperceptible.
Therefore, because there are two kinds of objects of cognition (*prameya*), two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are accepted.

Alternatively, the exclusion of the numbers three and one follows from the observation of two objects of cognition (*prameya*). If it is held that there is only one [object] because the non-existent (*asat*) is not an object of cognition, we agree with that;
however, there is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) regarding its being a non-object of cognition, since the existence of the non-existent is also ascertained.

That [cognition] is either a definitive means of valid cognition (*niścaya-pramāṇa*) or it is not a cognition born from the senses. For if a cognition were produced by the force of an object while disregarding the object's causal capacity, then sensory cognition would arise even when there is an obstruction or other such conditions.
If it is argued that the absence [of perception] constitutes the certainty of the non-existence of perception itself,
then that very absence is either a contradictory [reason] or a probans characterized by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*).
Furthermore, the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established for the sake of apprehending the consciousness of another.
Furthermore, because activity begins with regard to practical discourse (*vyavahāra*) and the like, the certainty of its existence is established.

It is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-discrepant; however, if it is argued that there is no confidence [in its validity] because it sometimes deviates, [we reply that] such a sign is not so, due to the faulty perception of those who do not see it correctly.
Since its cognition is sometimes established regarding a certain object,
that [cognition] must necessarily be either produced from it or have it as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
For an object cannot possibly exist without its own cause or its own intrinsic nature.
And whatever form is observed in those two, that very same thing is the defining characteristic elsewhere—

whether it be in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or in its own cause (*svanimitta*)— provided that the other causes of perception are present and the object itself is visible. But if the object is invisible, how can there be existence for that which possesses such a characteristic?
And if the cognition of a universal were invalid, its non-existence would follow,
just like [the non-existence of] existence after death (*pretyabhāva*). If it were perceived by the senses through a succession of moments,
that too is not possible, because sensory cognition cannot occur with respect to the capacity of the sense organs and so forth.
If there were a cognition of non-existence, it would be without a cause for the arising of that cognition.
Furthermore, perception regarding a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) occurs without conceptualization;
since the grasping of a universal (*sāmānya*) does not occur without conceptualization, inference [would be impossible] with respect to that [universal].
If the objects of cognition were restricted [to the three means of knowledge], the impermanence of color would not be cognized;
for that cognition would require another means of knowledge, since it cannot occur without a logical mark (*liṅga*),
as the relationship of the logical mark is not established in the case of "perception of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*).
That [inference] would be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) because of the multiplicity of objects to be known; or else,

there would be a multiplicity of means of valid cognition due to their occurring with respect to many [objects] or even a single one, just as in the case of "perception of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭi*), where there would be no exclusion of the numbers one or three.
Because there is no restriction regarding the object [of cognition] and because other objects of knowledge are possible,

this fault does not apply when there is a connection with the universal of color (*varṇasāmānya*). This is because it has been established that its nature is not non-existent, since it is proven to be so.

If it is argued that there is no establishment of another [object] elsewhere, we say no, because that very [object] is established. For whatever entity exists in a certain way, it becomes the cause for a cognition of a mark (*liṅga*) that corresponds to it; thus, from that, a cognition of the marked (*liṅgin*) arises regarding the entity as it truly is.

Thus, because there is a connection with the real object through a mediated succession of the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), there is no deception even though those two [cognitions] are devoid of the appearance of that [object];
for they determine the form of that [object], even though they themselves are devoid of its form.
Even when that form is non-deceptive, the establishment of error has been made [by others].
Therefore, when a real entity is to be cognized, the pervader (vyāpaka) is the cause for the cognition of the pervaded (vyāpya);
and that [cause] is either its own nature (svabhāva) or its efficient cause (kāraṇa), for it is the basis of that cognition.

But a negation is everywhere established through non-apprehension; for those who state the establishment [of a negation] by means of valid cognitions, it follows by implication from the opposite case. A statement of a contradictory property is observed either in that [negated object] itself or in its cause.
Even when there is a negation of that very thing, it is an indication of its lack of validity.

Otherwise, by stating the existence of one entity, how could the non-existence of another be understood? If you say it is because of contradiction, then that [contradiction] is also [to be explained].
