If it is argued that [non-existence] is established because of not being perceived together with [the object], from what is that known? If it is argued that it is because of the absence of perception of a perceptible thing, then that is simply non-validity (apramāṇatā).
Therefore, even though it is expressed by its own word, it is the establisher of non-existence.
That [non-existence] for which there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is in every way inexpressible;
by this, the statement of an effect that is contradictory to that [object] has been explained.
Only the formal application (prayoga) differs; the meaning does not differ in all cases.
That [statement] is contradictory, whether it fails to provide a means or does provide one; a statement of authority regarding a negation that does not follow logic—
such as the denial of an omniscient being, the existence of the afterlife, and so forth— is not in accordance with reason.
Since a contradiction between objects that transcend the senses is not established,
what relationship of sublated and sublator could there be between two cognitions based on reasoning?
If it is argued that such a contradiction exists because [the object] is not perceived, then let that very non-perception be the means of proof.

Such a non-perception has been described as producing uncertainty; for how could there be a definitive determination of existence or non-existence regarding those things that are absolutely beyond the senses?
Whether the property [used in the inference] is distinct or non-distinct from the subject, it is employed as a contradictory [reason].
Just as fire is the means for proving the absence of cold, or existence is the subverter of [the notion of] birth;
and just as a real entity alone is considered the means for establishing other real entities,
so too a real entity alone is the negator in the exclusion of other real entities.

By this [same principle], a property such as "being either the subject or one of its similar instances" (pakṣasapakṣānyataratva), which is merely projected by conceptual construction and could occur anywhere, is refuted; for even in that case, it is held that only a pervading property (vyāpaka-dharma) serves as the indicator of exclusion.

If the cessation of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) itself is somehow determined, then that very [cessation] is said to be the mark (*liṅga*) for the non-existence of the [pervader], which would otherwise lack a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*). However,
this is for the sake of those who are utterly deluded, for even a cowherd understands that [the absence of the pervader] follows from the non-perception [of the pervaded].
This much is the result of certainty: non-apprehension in the case of absence;

and that [occurs] when the reason or the essential nature (svabhāva) is considered invisible, yet is apprehended through inference from impermanence and so forth. This is the sequence held [to apply].
Validity alone [is what is apprehended], for it is not considered that there is grasping of what has already been grasped elsewhere.
There is no impermanence other than the entity itself, and that [entity] is established previously by means of the sense-faculties.
This [entity] is not to be expressed as having multiple forms; rather, it is the property (dharma) born of conceptual construction that is to be expressed.

When the substratum of a universal is fully established, that universal is indeed established. For when that [substratum] is not established, it is precisely through inference that this [universal] proceeds.
In some cases, there is a lack of full cognition of it, because of the possibility of another similar [instance].

Due to delusion, one who does not perceive the difference [between them] is like one who perceives a difference between an illusion and a wooden ball. For indeed, even a child, seeing that a lamp or similar object arises without connection to a subsequent moment and lacks any inferential mark [of permanence], certainly discerns it as perishable.

Even though the capacity exists as the very nature of the entity, there is delusion regarding the result because it is not immediately perceived; this is due to the lack of proficiency in the one who would determine it. For the sake of removing that very [delusion], inference is described.
Those of great intelligence discern all aspects through mere observation;
because it is excluded from everything else, cognitions based on that exclusion operate upon the object as if they were distinct, even though the object itself is undivided.
Just as the designations [of things] correspond to their verbal expressions, so too, in the absence of a cause for error,
one naturally connects mental representations (pratibhās) that conform to them by their own nature.
Alternatively, even in this case, destruction is established through the mark of non-perception.

For a thing that, having existed previously, no longer exists, is designated as "impermanent. Since the scripture speaks of impermanence as the connection with existence delimited by both ends, those two ends are recorded in the Smṛti as follows: [the beginning and the end].
If non-existence [of the entity] both before and after [its production] is what constitutes impermanence, why is that not simply impermanence itself?
If it is argued that this is because [the use of] the genitive case and so forth would be inappropriate, then how could that [non-existence] exist at the two ends [of the entity]?
Since existence and its relation [to time] are eternal, they cannot be qualified by the two ends.

If cause and effect were identical, there would be no distinction between them; since there is no connection [between them], he does not accept the prior non-existence of an entity. Furthermore, if those two [prior non-existence and posterior non-existence] are designated by means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), they—and that [entity] itself—are not established.
It is said that existence (*sattā*) is the cause because it effects its connection with its own causes;
yet both that existence and that relation are eternal. What, then, is the effect here, for which this non-existence could be produced? That [effect] is not an entity possessed of prior non-existence.
Because no relation [between word and object] is admitted, this entire universe is therefore eternal.

Consequently, even in the case of words intended to denote non-different objects, there are undesirable consequences (*anarthāḥ*): distinct conceptual cognitions (*dhiyaḥ*) arise based on exclusions (*vyatireka*) that differentiate the denotata (*vācya-bhedinyaḥ*), even though the words themselves are held to have non-different referents.
Recognition of specific features does not occur because of a difference at every moment;
nor does it have specific features as its object, since that [recognition] grasps them through similarity to what was seen before.
If it is argued that "that very same thing" is the illustration, then there is no apprehension of a universal.
Since it is already established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what further need is there for this illustration?
If you argue that there is no fault because it was forgotten, then that very thing is not an illustration.
If you claim that its existence is established through valid cognition upon seeing [the property] in another object, [we reply:]...
The superimposition of reality is error; because that [error] is established, it lacks the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since perception and its other [cognitions] are one, the establishment of one is the establishment of both. And they know that which is being synthesized by another to be a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) and a memory (*smṛti*).

If it is argued that [perception] is not [conceptual] because it depends on a sign (*liṅga*), that is not so, because memory is also [dependent on a sign and yet non-conceptual]. Perception is established as being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā-apoḍha*) by perception itself;
for all [beings], conceptualization based on names is known through self-awareness (*pratyātmavedya*).

Having withdrawn all thought from every side with a tranquil inner self, even while remaining [in that state], one perceives form with the eye; that is cognition born of the senses (akṣaja). Then, conceptualizing something again, one thinks: "Such was my conceptualization."
And because there is desire [for it], it is not the case that [the universal] is apprehended through the sense-faculty in the state previously described.
For a distinction observed in one place is not seen elsewhere;
therefore, there is no other distinct universal, because there is no difference in cognition.
Therefore, every cognition born of the senses has particulars as its object,
because the convention of words does not apply to particulars,
due to the lack of concomitance among particulars and the impossibility of establishing a convention for them.
Only that which is the object of words can be associated with them.

For when there is a relation expressed as "this belongs to that," the two objects that appear [in the cognition] are precisely those for which the relation exists; at that time, it is not within the range of the sense organs.
Because at that time the object does not appear with a clear manifestation,
and because the distinction between objects is determined by the difference in the appearance within consciousness;
even when the object appears to the eye, it is another [cognition] that declares "this belongs to this."
That [object] alone is joined with words; it is certainly not within the range of the senses.

For one whose senses have not been diverted [from the object], there is no manifestation [of the object] by mere speech regarding something else. Nor is there [cognition] for one who has not established the relationship [between word and object], because that would entail the consequence of self-cognition.
Because the conceptual and non-conceptual [cognitions] arise simultaneously in the two minds,
or because they arise so rapidly, the deluded person mistakes them for a unity.
Otherwise, perception would be interrupted by the intervention of conceptualization.
If this is argued, then how [is it explained] in the case of conceptualizations of different classes, or otherwise?

If the position that [the cognition] exists—like the perception of a whirling firebrand—is held to be stronger, then that applies equally elsewhere; or rather, there is the simultaneous hearing of two phonemes.
Although all objects have come into contact with the sense-faculties here at once,
that cognition which appears as if unobstructed even when there is an interval created by the five [senses] is called "mind" (*mati*), due to its being mixed with momentary cognitions at their limit.

If it is argued that the appearance is interrupted, then that [cognition] would be variegated; therefore, cognitions must indeed exist simultaneously. Furthermore, how could there be no distinction in the appearance between a preceding and a succeeding moment?
Moreover, in the case of pure mental conceptualization, there would be no perception of succession.
When the mind is attached elsewhere, there is no apprehension of an object even when it is present;
this objection applies to both [theories], because the production of another [cognition] is impaired by that attachment.
Furthermore, in the case of a whirling firebrand and the like, which function with great speed, [the cognition] obstructs the perception of continuity.
One perceives the illusion of a wheel through the visual faculty, not by the mere conjunction of those faculties.
Some say that because it arises from the sense organs and so forth, it is non-conceptual like the cognition of a child;
they claim that for children, the cause of conceptualization is a lack of proficiency in linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).
For those [who argue that perception is conceptual], it would indeed be direct perception for children because they lack conceptualization;
furthermore, even later on, that [perception] would not exist for them due to the absence of the means of linguistic convention.
If it is held that there exists a mind for which conventions have not been mastered, [then that must be the case].
In this way, [the same] would apply even to that which is born of the senses; and this [argument] is similar to the "remainder" (śeṣavat).
Whatever proof is used for a child, let that very same one be stated here as well.
By this, experience and so forth have been described on the grounds of the equality of sensory cognitions.
Having grasped the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and the worldly convention, and having synthesized these, one cognizes it in that way and not otherwise;
just as in the case of a man with a staff, because the genus and so forth are not determined through differentiation.
In that case, there is no connection with the possessor of that [universal], and therefore even conceptual construction does not exist here.
Even if cognition were continuous and appeared as the word and the individual,
it is described as "cowness" (gotva) because it is devoid of the forms of color, shape, and syllables.

Even though it is identical, that very [object] is not perceived as an object of the eye; because there is no appearance of two [distinct things], a difference in cognition is difficult to establish. Since inherence (samavāya) is not grasped by the senses, the non-perception of a relation remains established.
Furthermore, these expressions such as "the cloth is in the threads" are merely invented by oneself.
In common worldly usage, one says "the horn is on the cow," whereas "the cow is in the horn" is unworldly;
for no separation of the remaining parts designated as the "cow" is ever perceived.

With those threads, this cloth [is produced]; thus the subsequent effect is described. It is never simultaneous with the refinement of the threads, whether by way of superimposing the cause upon the effect or by way of a single conceptual abstraction.
One should apply the designation "thread" to the effect, demonstrating that it does not contradict the Vedic scripture;
for the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary exists either through a continuous connection or as a mere perception.
That which is the primary object of the initial linguistic convention is the cognition that is unerring.
Furthermore, there is no inference regarding a real entity that is differentiated by such categories as genus (jāti) and so forth;
for indeed, even the designation of things like a staff is based on the conventional (saṃvṛta).
Moreover, words such as "real entity" (vastu), "palace," and "row" do not depend on anything else.

If the house is a conjunction, then what indeed would that "garland" be? If it were a genus (*jāti*), then even a single house would have to be called a "garland," just as [a single] tree [is called a tree].
Furthermore, when there is a plurality of garlands, how could that word apply, since a genus cannot itself possess another genus?
Furthermore, regarding the "largeness" and so forth perceived in a garland and the like, which is held to be metaphorical:
it is not metaphorical because it is apprehended by a cognition that is indistinguishable from that of the primary [object].
That state of having no other cause is equal even in those things intended to be primary.

What other reason does the word *padārtha* consider besides the group of six? Whatever is established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is spoken of as such, whether it be primary or secondary; and even in the case of entities, the term is applied metaphorically to non-existence.
Conventional usage follows linguistic convention, and that convention follows the speaker's intention;
it is established for the sake of practical communication, like the names of meters, parts of words, or proper nouns.
Objects of experience are the causes of such cognition precisely by virtue of being the inherent properties of things.
Even when there is difference, that [object] is cognized as such because of the cognition of it;
likewise, even when cognitions are different, they are so through the reflective awareness of non-difference.
This is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the distinctness of effects, not of a single entity.
Therefore, because it exists in relation to real entities, verbal cognition (śruti) is based upon those entities;
even in the case of non-existence, that verbal cognition is based on the exclusion of external causal capacities.
It is fixed upon conceptual reflections (vikalpa-pratibimba) which themselves are based upon those [entities].

Therefore, because it is based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the word is said to perform the exclusion of others. That reflection of an object which appears in cognition as if it were distinct from the word—though it arises from the word—that too is not the essence of the object; it is an error born of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

When that [universal] is denoted by words, what part of its meaning is understood? And if it is not understood, the act of establishing a convention for its sake would be useless. Therefore, it is said that in this context, the word expresses a portion of the object, namely, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Furthermore, that mental aspect does not exist in the object; how then can one who asserts it be a partaker of the object?
That [aspect] is not concomitant with the object, yet it is the effect of the word which is concomitant with the object.
It is produced by the repeated practice of perception and arises from the non-differentiation of the cognition.
Furthermore, because there is an apprehension of what is excluded from others through the process of superimposing that form [onto the object],
this contradicts the statement that "the meaning of a word is that very [external] object. Alternatively, these cognitions produced by words have a false appearance.
Or rather, the word is said to produce exclusion (apoha) because it follows along with this portion of the meaning;
therefore, even at the time of convention,
exclusion from others (anyāpoha) is connected to the word as being associated with the indicated object, having its own cognition as the result.

Because it depends on the non-perception of others and because it depends on the perception of some, exclusion (apoha) is connected with the word; this is not applicable to a real entity (vastu). Therefore, universals (jāti) and so forth, as well as their connection, do not exist in the object, nor does the word apply to them.

It is joined [to the object] through the exclusion of others, because words themselves are applied [therein]. This [application] has the nature of a synthesis based on what is perceived, employing the means of recollecting the linguistic convention;
how could that exist in visual perception, which is devoid of reflection upon the preceding and the succeeding?
Even when the mind is directed elsewhere, one perceives a form with the eye;
there, the grasping of the linguistic convention is clear, and the conceptual construction arising from it occurs. Conceptual constructions arise only where a word has been applied.
Therefore, [if they were self-aware], the sense-born cognitions would proceed according to one's will and would not perceive external objects.
One would perceive "form, form," but why would one perceive that cognition?
Furthermore, there is an experience of it; how could that [experience] be non-conceptual?

When that very [consciousness] is experienced, two conceptual constructions are not seen simultaneously; by this, the experience of another consciousness occurring at the same time is refuted. Furthermore, memory would occur regarding what has passed; how could that [memory] arise if [the object] was not previously grasped?
Furthermore, the cognition of one's own thought would be of an undifferentiated form due to its being distinguished by another cognition;
and the perception of an object that is past—being without an example and without a logical mark—is established by what? For in that case, it is neither perceptual nor inferential.
If that [cognition] were grasped by an immediately succeeding cognition that manifests its own nature—
just as color and other objects are grasped— then there would be no apprehension of the preceding cognition.
That experience of consciousness regarding its own object is non-conceptual, just like [the perception of] color.
Just as that [non-conceptual cognition] cannot be subject to linguistic convention, so too other [objects] are beyond conceptualization.

Words denote universals (*sāmānya*), and conceptual construction has that single universal as its object. If non-conceptual [cognition] were absent, how could there be the apprehension of particulars (*viśeṣa*)?
If there exists something non-conceptual, it must have a cause similar [to other non-conceptual cognitions]; for the difference among effects arises from the difference in their causes.
[Conceptual cognition] does not depend on the external object for its connection [with words], but rather on the recollection of linguistic convention (*samaya*).
Likewise, the visual cognition [of color] occurs through the power of the object itself, independent of convention.
If color were dependent upon the recollection of convention in the sensory consciousness,
it would not be possible for it to appear without such dependence, just like a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the case of memory.

Since that [recollection] arises from its conjunction with that [object], would the sensory cognition arise from memory or not? If it were from memory, then it should occur even at a later time, since there might be some distraction [at that point].
If it is argued that both are causes occurring in succession, then [the cognition] should have occurred earlier, because there is no difference [in the causal conditions].
If it is argued that there is another cause for the cognition of the sense-faculties, then memory is likewise useless in that regard.
Just as the convention of "sameness" is accepted for the sake of establishing identity,
yet difference is actually perceived, what purpose would memory serve in that case?
When there is the apprehension of a mere universal, dependence upon particulars is not logical;
therefore, visual cognition arises in dependence upon both the eye and the form.
If the object were directly capable of producing cognition, it would be like the sense organ itself.
Now, why is it that its birth, which depends on both [the sense organ and the object], is not described by means of that [object]?
For a designation is not accepted unless its capacity to convey meaning has been examined;
and that capacity exists in the designation "sense organ" (akṣa), as does the property of being applicable to that [designation].
Therefore, in this designation, the nature of the [individual] mark (liṅga) is to be applied;
it ceases because the non-pervasive nature has ceased.
There, the aggregate is the collection, and the cognition of the sense-faculty is directed toward that universal (sāmānya).

And a cognition of a universal is necessarily cognized through conceptual construction (vikalpa). Those other atoms which arise from a connection with another object have been called "aggregated" (saṃcita), for they are indeed the cause for the production of cognition.
And that distinction among atoms does not exist without other [surrounding] atoms;
therefore, because there is no restriction to a single [atom], it was stated that cognition has the universal as its object.
Now, even if they occupy a single location, multiple [atoms] are not perceived simultaneously.
Is the appearance of simultaneous apprehension [seen] in the case of sesame seeds and the like when they are separated?

And has not the argument regarding "quickness" (lāghava) already been answered in the case of those very same [seeds] when they fall in succession? Why then is there no non-sequential apprehension, given that all cognitions are of equal duration?

Among those [cognitions], some appear to be non-successive while others appear to be successive; why is this so? Therefore, it follows that this [consciousness] would be non-successive when grasping all objects simultaneously. Furthermore, how could a single form, such as a variegated butterfly or the like, ever be perceived?
If it is argued that this single [entity] is variegated, then this is even more variegated than that;
for a single nature is not variegated, just like the form of a gem. Furthermore, the appearance of blue and other colors is the same in the case of a variegated cloth and so forth.
In that case, if only the form of the parts were perceived,
then you would perceive a "variegated" variegation distinct from blue and the other colors; yet this is not so,
because when two cognitions have identical objects, forms, and times, they are not observed as distinct.
How can one [cognition] have diverse objects and possess a sequence, while another has a single object and lacks sequence?
For it is through the very diversity of cognitions that the manifold nature of entities is established;
if that [diversity of cognitions] were not a factor, by what means would this systematic distinction between different things be proven?
Because heterogeneous atoms do not initiate [a new effect], there is no cognition of variegation in paintings and the like;
because it lacks form, conjunction is not variegated, nor is it the locus of such a figurative attribution,
since each [atom] individually is non-variegated and they are grasped sequentially.
There is no synthesis of a variegated cognition by means of a single [perception], because many [colors] are not apprehended by one [cognition].
Therefore, it is established that a single [cognition] has multiple objects; thus, even the final conclusion (siddhānta) is non-conceptual (avikalpikā).
For even while conceptualizing one object, one perceives another as well.
If unity is not tenable in the case of objects that appear as variegated,
then how can that very cognition— which appears as variegated— be one?
This is what the wise declare as being established by the force of reality itself.
To the extent that objects are analyzed, they fall apart to that same extent.
How could there be such diversity within a single cognition? Even in that [cognition], it would not exist.
If this [diversity] is what objects themselves find pleasing, then who are we in that matter?

Therefore, the appearance of grossness exists neither in objects nor in cognition, because such a nature has been refuted in the case of a single [atom]; it is likewise impossible in the case of many. This internal discernment appears as if it were an external part.
For the appearance of difference in cognition, which is itself non-different, is indeed an illusion.
Since even one of the two [subject and object] is absent therein, both are likewise lost. Therefore, the reality of that [cognition] is precisely its emptiness of duality.
And this establishment of the difference among entities is based upon that [cognition];
when that [cognition] is corrupted, their difference is also corrupted.
Furthermore, there exists no defining characteristic external to the forms of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject.
Therefore, because they are empty of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are revealed to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Every defining characteristic of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, in their specific details, is conditioned by activity (*vyāpāra*); and since that [activity] is not the reality (*tattva*), these [aggregates] are thus devoid of defining characteristics.

Just as for those whose minds are afflicted by ignorance, a representation arises with false aspects due to dependence on its own conditions— like [the vision of] those suffering from cataracts and the like— and that [representation] is not cognized in its true nature by all other philosophical systems.
Since those [external objects] are impossible without the delusions of the apprehended and the apprehender,
those who disregard the true nature of reality close their eyes like elephants and proceed with the investigation of the external solely according to worldly convention.
In a variegated cognition, the blue and other [colors] are attributes of the cognition and do not exist apart from it;
for they cannot be perceived [as separate], since one falls into [the error of perceiving them as external] objects by attempting to differentiate them.
In whatever manner a cognition appears, in that very same way it is manifested.
Thus, there would be a single state of being for the mind that possesses variegated forms;
likewise, if the form of a cloth and so forth were one, there would be no distinction. There is no intention to speak of what is distinct, nor does one perceive what is non-distinct.

Or what contradiction is there if many [causes], having produced an excellence (*atiśaya*), were individually to become the cause of cognition, provided they do not function like the self, the sense organs, and so forth? Apart from being a cause, there is no other such thing as "being an object of apprehension" (*grāhyatā*).
In that case, whatever appears in cognition is said to be its object of apprehension.
Or else, how could a whole be apprehended simultaneously with its own parts?
For a cognition of a cow is never observed when the dewlap and other such [parts] are not seen.
Even if it is accepted that the subordinate (guṇa) and the principal (pradhāna) are apprehended simultaneously,
the object would not be grasped with all its parts complete at once, nor as possessing the qualities and so forth [in their full extent],
because the status of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) or the qualified (viśeṣya) is dependent upon the speaker's intention.

For that which is apprehended as a constituent part is indeed grasped by that very [part] itself; because an entity is not distinct in itself from other things, and because qualities and so forth— which would serve as differentiators—
are not perceived, there would be no cognition of difference even for one who perceives one thing after another.

If it is argued that the cognition of multiplicity arises from the perception of distinctions such as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, let it be so; nevertheless, there would still be a confusion of their relations.
Since sound and other objects are manifold, the simultaneous perception of many [qualities] is established.
Because it is impossible to grasp a configuration without grasping the things that possess that configuration,
[the universal] is excluded from whatever it is excluded from; thus,
its differentiation is inferred from those exclusions, and this constitutes the manifold nature of the subject (*dharmin*).
Those imagined distinctions of form are not the object of a non-conceptual mind; for a variegated appearance belonging to a diverse [mind] that occurs only occasionally cannot be its domain.
Even if whiteness and so forth exist in whatever manner they are objects of the senses, [they are not the object of such a mind].
That [object] is not denoted by words because of the difference in the forms of cognitions.
Even if cognitions have a single object, if you claim they possess different substrata,
then why are the minds of the listener and others not now considered to have different objects?
The basis for the various cognitions that arise from a single object is indeed one and the same;
how then can that [single] form appear with diverse aspects?
This is because the verbal designation and the conceptualization do not apprehend the perceived object during their occurrence.
Through the observation [of the object], recognition of cows and the like is refuted;
and that inference of genus and so forth from the concomitance of the name and the conceptual construction regarding the visible cow and such is likewise invalidated by this same [argument].
It has been explained that even distinct perceptions, by their very nature, produce a single conceptual construction known as recognition; however,
if this involves the apprehension of what was previously experienced, it lacks the status of valid cognition for the mental faculty.

If [the sense organ] were to grasp what is unperceived, even the blind and others would perceive objects. Furthermore, because [the object] is momentary, its perception is impossible once it has passed away. If it were non-momentary, then a definition with a qualification would have to be stated.

Why is it maintained that a sense-organ or any other means of accomplishment is required for an object when its function has already been fulfilled, and it does not produce any further distinction? Moreover,
all cognitions arising from that [object] would have to occur simultaneously.
Because there is no contradiction in its dependence on that [preceding moment], even though it does not produce a different effect than others;

therefore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), arising from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) of sensory perception, apprehends a distinct object, and for that reason, it is not blind.
Sensory cognition is a cause that depends precisely upon the connection with its own object;
therefore, even when it apprehends something else, it is considered to have a restricted range of objects.
How could that [object], which does not exist at the time of its own cognition, be simultaneous with the activity [of the cognition]?
If it is argued that the object serves as a cooperative cause for the sensory cognition, [we reply:
no, because that which is non-existent lacks capacity prior [to the cognition], and because it is of no use afterward;
therefore, all causes must exist beforehand, and thus the object does not coexist with its own cognition.
If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be the object of apprehension,
those who know the logic of the matter understand that its status as an object consists simply in its being the cause capable of imparting its form to the cognition.
For an effect, even when arising from multiple causes, emerges by conforming to one of them.
It is said that the [cognition] grasps that form as it was presented by that [object];
for the nature of passion and the like cannot be associated with linguistic convention, as it does not partake of anything else.
Therefore, their self-awareness is not accompanied by verbal expression (*abhijalpa*).
Since they do not know even another's [nature], how can they know their own nature?
Some say they are known by a cognition residing in the same object.
Entities possess either that form or its opposite because they are produced from causes that possess either that form or its opposite.
Is that pleasure and so forth non-cognition, or is it produced from causes non-different from those of cognition?
When the object is present, the sense organ is capable, and the respective mind is also present, the arising of pleasure and so forth is observed; this is the same for cognitions as well.

Whether these [causes] exist or do not exist, neither birth nor non-birth is ever observed anywhere for pleasure and so forth, or for cognition; therefore, they [arise] from those [causes] and not from anything else. Furthermore, the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth, arises specifically from the particularity of those very [causes].
Just as there are degrees of dullness and acuity belonging to that very cognition,
how could that [cognition] apprehend pleasure and so forth alone, while excluding the object by whose presence those cognitions of pleasure and so forth were produced?
If there were a perception of succession, that cognition would not appear as uninterrupted.
If you argue that this is due to the rapidity [of the process], then why is it not the case that there is no cognition at all, since that [rapid succession] applies equally?
Furthermore, two things cannot be known by a single sensory consciousness, because of the restrictive rule governing the mind of the senses.

Even in the absence of pleasure and so forth, [the universal] arises from the object; yet that [pleasure] is not established as having that [objective] power. Furthermore, if both [the object and the pleasure] possessed their own distinct capacities, then pleasure would be perceived alone, like blue and other [colors], even for one who does not perceive its cause.
For it is not logical that there be a cognition [of the mind] when [it is] grasped together with the object itself;

what capacity do pleasure and so forth have [in this regard], since the cognition is not accepted as arising from them? If pleasure and so forth were experienced by means of the eyes and other [senses] without an object, [this would be absurd].
Color-form and the like, as well as the distinctions of "woman" and so forth, would never be perceived by the sense organs.
For when an internal object is present, the cognition produced by the sensory power does not perceive external things;
thus, when an object is being apprehended, there would be no awareness of pleasure and the like that arise from it.
If cognitions were to arise simultaneously, then because their respective objects would be present together,
there would be the simultaneous experience of pleasure and pain whenever an object is encountered.
Even if an internal material cause (*upādāna*) exists, the occurrence of suffering and so forth would still take place within consciousness.
If it is thought that [the preceding moment] is the material cause (*upādāna*) of that which is contradictory to it, and yet they are one,
then by what means could consciousness be the material cause of non-consciousness?
However, it is observed that [a cause] may exercise sovereign influence (*ādhipatya*) even over that which is contradictory to it.
Just as a single light simultaneously produces both the impairment and the non-impairment of the visual perception of form for a night-prowler and for others,
so too do pleasure and the other [mental states] [arise from objects] that appear as having been transferred into their own [form].
And for these [cognitions], their own self is the knower, and their birth is solely from objects.

For the nature of the object, having become their own self, is experienced by them. Therefore, there is the designation of "experience of the object," while the objective support is merely the appearance of that [object].

Someone might say that pleasure and so forth, which are external and insentient, are the objects of perception; yet for such a person as well, the simultaneous apprehension of both [the object and its cognition] is not logical. If blue and so forth are apprehended simultaneously because they are non-different in nature from pleasure and so forth, [then the same fault follows].
If the two cognitions appear as distinct, how could their object be non-distinct? If that [object] were without distinction, then despite the varying degrees of mental cultivation,
there would be no variation in the intensity of pleasure and pain within the cognition.

If there is no contradiction even for cognition because it has pleasure and so forth as its nature, then how is it understood that this [object] is external and has pleasure and so forth as its nature? If you say it is because the grasped and the grasper belong to different classes, [we reply: no.
It would be a non-apprehender of anything; consequently, its status as an enjoyer would be lost.
By this, the relationship of cause and effect is refuted in that which is neither cause nor effect;
for in the absence of the relation of apprehended and apprehender, that [causality] would have to exist elsewhere as well.
Therefore, those [mental factors] are indeed internal, and they are conscious because they are objects of awareness.
That which is not of the nature of awareness cannot be the experience of that [object].
If it is argued that an experience not having that [external object's] intrinsic nature nevertheless apprehends those mental states belonging to the mind (buddhi), [we reply: no.
Apart from consciousness whose form is perceived through direct perception and memory, what other cognition could there be here?
Various experiences of pleasure, pain, and so forth are seen to arise as a single [cognition] without taking up those various objects; nothing else is observed in between.
If it is argued that there is no distinction due to conjunction, as in the case of an iron ball and fire,
then the established distinction between difference and non-difference would be destroyed in all things;
for while that which is perceived as non-distinct is a unity, that which is not so [perceived] possesses distinction.
If this [cognition] were not a means of proof, the proof for difference would not be established.
White, suffering, and so forth appear as distinct, yet they are non-different from the cognition that perceives them.
If [you claim] that what appears non-differently is actually distinct, then upon what could difference and non-difference depend?
Because even when [objects] are obscured by something sharp, a distinction is sometimes perceived,
the establishment of the difference between the cognitions in a continuous stream is proven.
That aforementioned knowledge of yogins is due to their cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
When the web of conceptual construction has been shaken off, reality appears with perfect clarity.
Those afflicted by desire, grief, fear, madness, thieves, dreams, and the like,
perceive even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them.
That which is bound up with conceptual construction cannot manifest as a clear object;

even in a dream, it is remembered as something remembered, and such [a memory] appears as if it were an actual object. Furthermore, things such as the meditation on the foul or the "earth-totality" (pṛthivī-kṛtsna) are described even though they are not real.
That which is produced by the power of meditative cultivation appears clearly and is free from conceptual construction;
therefore, whatever is intensely cultivated— whether real or unreal—
yields as its fruit a cognition that is vivid and non-conceptual upon the completion of that cultivation.

In that regard, that [cognition] which is consistent with reality, like an object previously determined, is accepted as perception arising from the cultivation of that [object]; all others are distortions.
Wherever a cognition grasps the meaning of a word, it is conceptual construction in that respect.

And the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) is not the object of a word; therefore, all [cognition] therein is direct perception (adhyakṣa). Thus, there are four kinds of cognition that appear as direct perception: three types of conceptual cognition arising from a defect in the basis (āśraya-upaplava), and one non-conceptual [cognition].
The two [types of perception] were stated for the purpose of establishing that [perception] is not produced by the senses; however, because error is observed,
the mention of inference and so forth is solely for the sake of proving those two former ones,
in order to exclude the conceptualization that superimposes other objects based on linguistic convention.
Because it is the cessation of what is not present to perception, it is sometimes a cause of error;
just as this conceptualization of an imperceptible object, such as memory and the like,
depends upon convention and does not ascertain the object through direct perception.
Likewise, without the recollection of what was previously experienced, there would be no subsequent cognition regarding jars and the like; and that [recollection] is lost through perception.
Therefore, the fourth [type of error] here is an exception, and it is said to be produced by an impairment [of the sense organs].
In that case, some maintain that the visual impairment (*timira*) is merely an indicator of an injury,
and that even this [cognition] is mental; however, their position contradicts their own text,
which states that the sense organs are also the cause of cognitions such as the blue color or the double moon.
If it is argued that [the object] is the cause through a succession [of moments], then while the domain of sensory cognition is being investigated, what relevance is there here for mental cognition?
Or, if [mental cognition] conforms to the presence or absence of the senses, how could it be considered sensory?

If it is argued that this [cognition] is similar to that [error] because it involves a modification, why is this not denied just as that is? Furthermore, like the error regarding a snake and so forth, this [cognition] would persist even when there is no modification of the sense organ; its cessation would not occur even when the impairment of the sense organ has ceased.
Sometimes, even when such [objects] exist in another continuum, they would depend upon the perception and recollection of those who express them; they would not appear with perfect clarity.
Whether in one who is asleep or awake, that cognition alone which appears with vivid clarity [is the one in question].

That [cognition] is non-conceptual in both ways, yet otherwise it is indeed conceptual; therefore, even though it is non-conceptual, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is denied because of its lack of correspondence with reality. And for that reason, what appears to be perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) is declared to be of two kinds.

It is not the case that everything is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for every action; for that which is the action itself cannot be its own means of accomplishment. In this regard, by virtue of mere experience, cognition possesses a nature similar [to its object].
That by which [the cognition] is differentiated according to each respective object must be its own nature;
for a difference that does not constitute its own nature, even if it exists within the causes,
cannot serve as the regulator for a non-differentiated [cognition] with respect to differentiated objects.
Therefore, since its own differentiation is its apprehension,
this restriction of the object for the action is established; that [apprehension] is proven by that [differentiation],
for it connects this [cognition] with the object without abandoning the form of the object itself.
Even if another factor were somehow a differentiator of cognition from its own internal distinctions, nevertheless,
it is the conformity to the object (*meyarūpatā*) that is the means for the apprehension of the object of knowledge;
for if the means were something else, its connection with that object would not be established.

And since that [cognition] is indeed its very self, the result is not a separate entity from it. And that [cognition], while producing that [result] within itself in the form of the apprehension of the object, appears as if possessed of activity with respect to its own object by means of that activity.
Because it is established through the power of that [cause], although it is itself not an agent,
it is described in the world as possessing activity due to its grasping the form of the cause, since it arises with a nature similar to those causes of the fruit.

Therefore, because of the intervention [of other factors] with respect to the action, validity is not accepted for these: the initial perception, the contact of the sense organ, and the cognition of the qualifier;
even though all these causal factors (kārakas) are employed toward the action.
That which is the ultimate differentiator of that [cognition] is considered its most effective means of proof (*sādhakatama*).
Since the sense organs are the causes of all general cognitions, they do not possess such [a specific differentiating capacity].
For even when there is a difference in those [organs], how could there be the notion "this belongs to that" regarding a cognition that remains undifferentiated?
By this, the remainder is explained: furthermore, if the cognitions of qualifiers do not possess that same form, there is no difference [between them] either;
or else, even for other cognitions, no distinction of object is admitted between the two, namely the action and its means.

If there were a single object, both [the subject and the predicate] would be redundant, and there could be no sequential occurrence; if the two parts of the cognition were to arise simultaneously, there would be an absence of the relationship between the probandum and the probans.
It is by relying upon that [sequential distinction] as its basis that the establishment of the probandum and the probans is maintained.
Even when connected with its entire essence, it would be perceived only by certain [cognitions] through specific properties;
such a restriction would not exist because the connection itself is without distinction.
Yet, even though there is no difference in that [connection], this distinction exists because of the validity of that [cognition].

If it is argued that [the effect arises] from a conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*), then [the objection of] "not having that nature" does not apply, because that [conditioning factor] is also not established [as distinct].
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between the action and the instrument being one and the same, that is incorrect;
for while a distinction between properties (*dharma*) is admitted, the underlying entity (*vastu*) is held to be non-different.
In this way, the entire system of actions and their factors (kārakas) functions through superimposition upon entities that are actually conceived as non-different.
What, then, is the cognition of an object? It is simply this direct perception, which is the individual awareness [of the object].
By what means is there the cognition of that object? Since it possesses the same form [as the object], how can it be non-deviant?
Or, if that [cognition] is the experience [of the object], where is this [object]? This very point is being investigated:
by what means do those atoms possess a similar form, and how is there the appearance of something gross?
Therefore, its possessing the form of the object is not invariably concomitant with a real object;
it is thus incapable of establishing the existence of the cognition of that [object].
If [it is argued that] similarity to that [object] and arising from that [object] constitute the definition of being cognized, [then...]

The object of cognition would be the immediately preceding consciousness (samanantara-vijñāna) which shares the same object; that upon which the determinative cognition (*avasāya-dhī*) arises—namely, "this was seen," "this was heard," or "this was known"—is its experience (*anubhava*). That very proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is now being examined.
That by which the seen and the seeing are established is considered the means of proof for that [consciousness].
Relying upon the relationship between those two, this determination belongs to the seer.
That is its self-experience, and it does not belong to anyone else.
Its being directly perceived is also its identity with that [cognition]. There is no other object to be experienced by it, nor is there any other experience of it;
for since the same objection applies equally to that [other experience], it is that very [cognition] which shines forth by itself.
This [cognition] has blue and other forms as its intrinsic nature, and it is also an experience;
thus, while being an experience of its own nature, it is known as the "experience of blue" and so forth.
Being manifest, it illuminates its own nature because of their identity (*tādātmya*).
Just as illumination is accepted [to be self-revealing], so too is cognition the knower of itself.
And for that [cognition], if another object were to be known, the roles of the known and the knower would be difficult to establish.
Thus, it is perceived by the deluded as having the forms of both the known and the knower.

When this [consciousness], which has not established a distinction, is subject to the delusion of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender characterized as separate— as in the case of the various cognitions of [illusory] hairs and the like— then it cannot be challenged on the grounds of having the characteristics of an apprehended object and an apprehending subject.
In that case, since there is no other consciousness, self-consciousness (svasaṃvit) is accepted as the result.
If an external object were experienced, what fault would there be? None at all.
Would this not simply mean that the external object is experienced?
If cognition possesses that form, then it must contain that form;
this deserves investigation as to whether it [arises] from an external object or from something else.
For that which is devoid of the limiting condition of perception is not apprehended, whereas when that [condition] is apprehended, it is apprehended.
The perception appears as blue; there is no external object existing in isolation. For someone, something internal alone serves as the awakener of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, the restriction of cognitions does not depend upon an external object.
Therefore, there exists a single [cognition] possessing two forms, which is thus experienced and remembered; the awareness of this [cognition] in its dual aspect is the result.
This is so when another object—whether desired or undesired—is established as having that nature.
The object is the cause of the representation, and its experience is likewise so;
when cognition possesses an object because the object is established within a portion of the cognition itself,
then that very self-experience is the determination of the object.
Whether the self is experienced as having a desired form or otherwise,
whether it be desired or undesired, by that [experience] the object becomes known.
Even though an external object exists, it is known exactly according to the experience.
The self is determined by its own nature, for there is the fault of [the self] having multiple natures.
If the external does not exist, of what would there be cognition?
If, out of necessity, it is the nature [of cognition itself], why is it not considered to be the external?
Even if there were a means [of perception], there would be no distinct experience of the two [the object and its form].

If you say it is not so because of the obscuration of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), then the cognition would not be under the control of the object. [Such a cognition] would present that entity, which possesses a manifold nature, as having a single nature.

How, then, could that unperceived [cognition] be the knower of the object? If conceptual constructions— which manifest as desired and undesired things— are not sensory cognitions, then it is observed that even in those cases, the mind does not engage with the undesired and so forth.
Therefore, even when the object of cognition is external, it is logical that self-awareness (*sva-anubhava*) is the result,
because the determination of the object occurs exactly according to its own nature.
At that time, its very appearance as the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not [the external object], even though it exists.
The nature of the grasper is required in relation to external objects because it does not serve another's purpose; for,
just as that object-nature is established within the cognition,
so too is it determined by the self-awareness [of the subject] that "it is established in this way."
Thus, the cognition of the object is itself what is intended, because the nature of the object is not seen [independently].
For that [cognition], the object placed within the intellect is the means, and that [placement] is its activity.
For in whatever way that object is placed [within the intellect], in that very way it is manifested.
Because the establishment of the object consists in that [cognition], self-awareness is also considered to be awareness of the object.
Therefore, even if there is a difference in the objects, self-awareness is not the result;
for it was stated in the investigation of intrinsic nature that the awareness of the object is identical with it.
Even if the object is the cause of a cognition that appears in such a way— whether resembling [the object] or otherwise— the object's status as an object of cognition (*prameyatā*) is accepted;
for in no way is its having the form of the object tenable when it appears through reasoning.

Although the nature of cognition is indivisible, it appears as if possessed of the distinctions between the grasped object, the grasping subject, and the act of awareness, due to the distorted vision of those whose faculties are impaired by mantras and the like— just as a clod of earth appears [as something else] to those whose senses are affected by such spells.
They appear in one way even though they are devoid of that form,
because they are perceived exactly so by those whose eyes are unimpaired;
or just as in deserts, even a large object is seen as small when it is at a distance.

And just as this establishment of the object of cognition, the means of cognition, and the result is made according to how they appear— even though the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the consciousness itself do not [ultimately] exist—
otherwise, for a single entity appearing in various forms, [there would be no consistency].
True, but how could there be aspects, since that would entail the loss of its unity?
And because the other [aspect] would lose its distinctness, there is no non-difference, for we do not perceive formless things.
Indeed, it is by perceiving the non-difference of form that the intellect determines non-difference.
That form by which entities are determined does not exist in reality,
because neither a single nor a manifold form is found in them;
it is only through the observation of similarity that what is called "error" arises in the world.

In this world, there is no such thing as the determination of identity with respect to that which does not possess that nature, because even a single entity of that nature is not observed here. Furthermore,
this [determination] which arises from an internal affliction is also [unreal].
By its very nature, that [cognition] arises from defects and appears falsely,

independent of the perception of similarity and so forth, like the visual impairment known as *timira*. In that case, the determination of the cognition is considered to be the form of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*).
Because it is identical with that [self], the knower of the self is that [cognition]; therefore, it is the means of its own proof.

In that regard, regarding the cognition of the self, just as the experience of passion and so forth [is the means], this establishment of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result should be applied everywhere.

In that case as well, because they consist of the nature of experience, they are capable of self-awareness; thus, that capacity is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the self is the object of cognition (*prameya*), and self-awareness is the result (*phala*). The nature of determination within the self is designated as the form of the apprehender.
And that fitness is said to be the means of valid cognition, which is self-awareness. For every cognition indeed arises from objects;
even if there were another cause, how could it possess the form of the object?
Just as, although food, time, and other factors are causes for the birth of offspring,
the child assumes the form of one of the parents and not that of any other;
so too, although [the sense organs] are equal in being causes of that [cognition], it is held that [the cognition] has an object other than those [organs].
The status of being an object [of cognition] depends on that [external thing]; in its absence, that [status] would not exist.
Even in a consciousness possessing an object, there might be the suspicion that it has the form of a non-object.
Once the grasping of a past object is established, the self-cognition of the two-fold nature [of the cognition] is proven.
Because it is differentiated by the appearance of blue and so forth, the object is not a universal (jāti) that lacks those qualities;
nor can that [universal] be impermanent, for it would then not be a universal, or if it were permanent, how could it be a producer?
Names and the like have already been refuted previously; this sequence does not apply to things that possess real meaning.
Because it follows merely from one's desire, the capacity of the object is not established.
Furthermore, memory is a cognition of this kind, and its arising occurs from experience;
since that [experience] was devoid of the form of the object, how can this [memory] now possess it?

At that time, the existence [of the object] does not arise from the object itself because it is absent; even if there were such an experience, that form would not belong to the object, because it is distinct from the clear form [of the object]. Furthermore, another person would likewise perceive that form as being separate [from the object].

If there were an eternal connection with the self, it would not be perceived even when [the word] is uttered. Furthermore, if there were a single connection between one [word] and one [self], the mental synthesis (*pratisandhi*)—
which consists of the two minds of the speaker and the listener being directed toward a single object— would not be possible.

If that single conventional usage [of "pot"] is due to similarity between two things that do not appear as such [i.e., as similar], then how could an object with a distinct nature be grasped? At that time, the cognition would be devoid of an object.
And that experiential consciousness depends upon both factors.
It is connected with that cognition by way of a specific single form;
for otherwise, how could that which lacks such a form ascend into the cognition?
Thus, each subsequent cognition possesses a single form, and likewise each succeeding one.
Its two forms— the form of the object and some form of itself—
are indeed distinguished by a third cognition;
for if there were a recollection of the object within the recollection of the cognition because it is the effect of the object, [then the following would hold].

The synthesis [of the object] occurs through error, and that [error] would exist in the case of light and mental attention (manaskāra). Likewise, there would be a perception [of all things] by means of their causes;
consequently, a jar would not be remembered as distinct from the potter and other such factors.

Because of that excellence [of the object] by which cognition becomes the vessel for the connection with the object, how could that [excellence] be anything other than similarity (*sārūpya*)? For this is seen in the case of twins and the like. Indeed, if [cognition] were of neither form [neither resembling nor not resembling the object], it would remain fixed in a single form.

The second [moment] would not be distinguished by the reflective consciousness (*parāmarśa-cetas*), because the intellect, which lacks the synthesis of objects, does not apprehend a second [moment]. Therefore,
it is the intellect appearing in the form of blue and so forth that stands before [the mind].
Otherwise, only the very first [cognition] would be conjoined with the object, because of the possibility of its existence;
the subsequent cognitions would not have a perceived connection with the preceding object,
since that which is being cognized simultaneously must necessarily be [conjoined] with the intellect.
By what form, then, is the distinctness of the object established?

Furthermore, difference would be perceived by erroneous cognitions, just as [duality is seen] in the non-dual moon. There is no rule of simultaneous perception for two distinct things, such as blue and yellow.
No object whatsoever exists without being cognized, nor is there any cognition of a non-object;
that which is being cognized is thus perceived, and between these two there is no distinction.
Therefore, it is impossible to prevent the appearance of an object at the time of its cognition.
The non-distinctness [of cognition] from knowledge would be the inference of a difference in causes; for,
even when other causes are present,
there is an absence of sensory cognitions if one does not state a restriction based on the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The production of a sprout from a seed, and the establishment of fire from smoke— such is the proof [of external objects]. Even that state of being an agent or a signifier which relies upon external objects, that too consists of cognitions appearing in those forms and occurring with such fixed regularity.

If it were postulated by relying on the intellect (buddhi), what contradiction would there be? Smoke might be produced from what is not fire; thus, there would be no inference of a cause from its effect. Or, even if causality exists, how could there be a certain (ekāntataḥ) inference [of the specific cause]?
In that case as well, a cognition appearing as smoke would lead only to a cognition appearing as fire— possessing a latent impression (vāsanā) potent enough to awaken it—
and not to the actual fire itself;
for [the cognition] contains within it a latent impression suitable for that [fire], which causes it to appear as smoke.
The mental continuum manifests cognition, just as smoke [manifests] fire; therefore, this is the doctrine of the learned. However, it is described by relying on external objects.
Its dual nature is established through the rule of simultaneous perception.

Cognition, bearing distinct appearances— such as sharp, dull, or turbid— with respect to a single object due to the differences in the sense faculties, is observed [to vary]. Since the object possesses an undifferentiated nature, the mental consciousness would have to be of a single form.
If all that [cognition] is for the sake of the object because of its objective reference, yet it lacks the appearance of that [object], then—
since it arises based on the object and conforms to its form—
it would still possess some degree of distinction from other [objects].
For in this way, although a son takes after his father, even while depending upon him,
he maintains a distinction from the father in certain respects;
[just as a peacock's eye] has the form of a peacock's eye (candraka), shining with blue and red.
Those with dim vision perceive a halo around lamps and such objects;
if that halo were an external form, why would those with clear vision be unable to see it? Furthermore, how could one who perceives a real entity be considered to have impaired faculties?

When his eye, purified of cataracts, clearly perceives an object beyond the senses that is visible to other eyes, how could that same object again be unclear to another person, given that [perception] arises from light,
the eye, and mental attention, which are the same for both?
The causal capacity is the cause; therefore, it is not something other than that, nor is the object a non-cause. If that very [object] is the cause of cognition, why does it depend on a lamp?
Since [cognition] exists by means of the lamp alone, neither [the object nor the lamp] is the [sole] cause.
It is not logical that there should be a distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest based on differences such as distance and proximity.

If it is argued that this distinction arises from differences in light, then in the cases of its being covered or uncovered, the perception or non-perception would be identical; for some minute part of it [would remain constant].
If it is argued that there is a distinction because an object is not seen when the light is dim,

then if the external object were a single unity, from where would the distinction between being seen and not seen arise? And if it were manifold, being divided into atoms, from where would the distinction between being seen and not seen arise?
If it is argued that the difference in cognition arises from the appearance [of the object] as undifferentiated despite differences in clarity and dimness,

then how can there be an appearance of something undifferentiated through a distinction when another thing is different? Furthermore, why is that light not also dim, given that there is an obscuration here?
Because fire is subtle, this [non-perception] occurs; however, elsewhere there is no such subtlety.
And when it is very near, that fire would be clearly manifest and exceedingly distinct.
If, even in that case, another form were to arise by depending on the unseen (adṛṣṭa), [then the following would apply].

Because they mutually obstruct one another, there would be an impairment of light; consequently, only one [object] would be seen. If that [light] were not obstructed, one would see the form clearly all at once. Or, if it were obstructed by the unseen [atoms], one would see the form both clearly and unclearly.
If that by which benefit and harm are not established does not exist, what could the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) possibly do?
Therefore, consciousness, arising in dependence upon objects according to their causes, assumes various appearances; all other [theories] are merely the fallacious arguments of the dull-witted.
Since knowledge, words, lamps, and perception— whether direct or otherwise—
are momentary and perish as soon as they arise,
how could there be a manifestation of things that are non-existent and provide no assistance to the cognition?
If it were argued that every object would be manifested in the manifestation [of the cognition] because that [manifestation] is its cause,
this conceptualization is also untenable; for a cognition is said to manifest an object by virtue of the appearance of that object within the cognition,
even when that object is absent, since that [appearance] is produced by it.

Furthermore, another object that has arisen simultaneously does not impart its form [to cognition], because it provides no assistance. If it does not impart its form, how can a manifest object— such as a diamond or a stone— which is stable and independent of anything else, appear with its own form in cognition?
If [the cause were permanent], it would produce all cognitions of the world simultaneously;
however, those [cognitions] arise sequentially for this [cause] due to the assistance of auxiliary factors.
They say that there is a difference [in the cause] at every moment; in this case too, the fault is the same as before.
There is no dispute among anyone regarding the identity of cognition;
its possessing the form of the object is established, and that too is proven by memory.
This is because it is not experienced as distinct [from the object], being differentiated from its own objects by means of distinct divisions.
If one were to say, "It is thus," or "It is certainly not thus," that [cognition] would not be non-differentiating;
nor does any distinction become discerned by mere experience alone. Furthermore, when the difference is unclear—as in the case of twins—the intellect is not discerning.
Self-awareness is also established for the most part by the proof of the two-fold nature [of cognition],
because at that time the manifestation that constitutes its own nature is observed as being cognized.
If cognition were known by another cognition of a different nature, then once that [original] cognition has ceased, from what would experience arise?

It does not know its own form; thus, the experience of the seeker is lost. Furthermore, that cognition appears directed toward the external, as if manifesting the object, whereas the cognition that apprehends the [preceding] cognition is always inwardly directed toward itself.

If it is argued that even though [the cognition] knows that which appears as its object, it does not know the object itself, what other consciousness could there be [to establish this], since [consciousness] is thought to consist in having that same form (*tādrūpya*)? If so,
it follows that all things possessing similar forms would mutually possess one another's consciousness.
If it is argued that cognition is similar to its object and that [cognition] is the knower of that [object], then [the cognition] would not now be similar to the knower itself.
That self-experience (*anubhava*) of it is not caused by similarity;
rather, in the world, that [self-experience] is the basis for the established distinction between action and its object.

The designation "experienced" for blue and so forth arises from the delusion of superimposition upon the cognition of that form which has become its very nature; it does not arise from an experience of another self distinct from the experience itself.
If the cognition possesses the form of blue and so forth, what proof is there for an external object?
If cognition does not possess a form such as blue and so forth, how can it be the experience of that [object]? When the nature of consciousness is not based on similarity of form,
since that [nature] is established for it by itself, what is brought about by the object?
For if there were complete identity in every respect, cognition would become non-cognition;
yet if there were similarity in some respect, everything would be the cognition of everything.
Just as the experience of blue and so forth is considered to occur because of the possession of the form of blue and so forth.
If it is argued that because it has the nature of experience, there must also be an experience of that [cognition],
and that the determination of it is like the object— meaning that the cognition is not unexperienced,
and therefore there is no fault— [we reply: No, for this [determination] exists at all times even with respect to the object.
Or why would it not exist in the experience itself, given that existence is the very basis [of cognition]?
Furthermore, this clear cognition— which appears to people as the manifestation of whiteness and so forth when something white or similar is being perceived— [is the proof].
Is that [manifestation] the form of another, such as white and so forth, or is it the form of itself?
If it were the form of another, then while the manifestation remains unilluminated, how could the white [object] be manifested?
Manifestation is cognition; if that [cognition] is not manifested, then the entire world remains unmanifested.

Because the same fault would follow even if one manifestation were manifested by another manifestation; and how could that [perception] distinguish an object whose relation [to the word] is unknown? For when one of two things is apprehended, there is no perception of the second.

If two things were seen in conjunction, there would be the certainty that "it has been seen. If it is claimed that the designation "seen" applies when an object of similar form is perceived by another cognition, then, given this similarity of form (*sārūpya*), its self-cognition (*svavedana*) is established.
Now, if one does not know the nature of the self, how can there be knowledge of the nature of another?
Furthermore, that cognition is designated as "perception" due to similarity has already been established.
Indeed, the apprehension of similarity occurs only between two things that have been seen, yet [the opponent] has not seen the object.
How could he determine its similarity with the [object] through perception beforehand? Furthermore, one who does not accept similarity cannot perceive both [the object and the cognition].
Thus, the discussion regarding "this is the object" and "this is the cognition," and their being known, has come to an end.
Now, if it is its own nature [that is consciousness], then it must manifest by itself;
for if that [nature] were not manifest, the object would remain unmanifest.
By this, those who hold the position of one who does not know the self [the non-Buddhists] are refuted, since they maintain that all objects are unseen [by consciousness].
Those who claim that cognition is imperceptible have also been answered above.
Cognitions, which function differently due to differences in their basis, objects, and habitual practice,
are indeed nothing but cognitions, distinguished as pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth.

That [object] is perceived directly, and nothing else distinct from it is discerned; if another person were to know it by means of some other [cognition], that cognition would either be produced from that [object] or have its appearance [of it]. If [it is argued that] another cognition does not know [the object], [then the object remains unperceived by others].

Even for another [cognition] that takes it as its object, these two [properties] necessarily exist. If, however, [the universal] does not arise from that [particular], then that cognition—which appears as that [universal]—is rendered objectless; and furthermore, if it is not apprehended, the universal itself cannot be apprehended.
It is said that [the object] is not apprehended, yet there is no such thing at all.
Therefore, this appearance of the object is not something other than that cognition;
thus, when the self-awareness of the nature of direct perception is established, it then apprehends that [object].
If it is argued that [the object] is not perceived [by the cognition], from what does this distinction between two capable [factors] arise?

If the restriction of consciousness is due to its connection with an unseen single object and so forth, then another [person] would never perceive it; thus, even the distinction between cognitions is refuted.

Furthermore, those yogins who perceive the pleasure and so forth of another through direct perception would likewise become afflicted, since they possess an experience identical to that [of the afflicted person],
even though that [affliction] arises for them from the absence of contact between sense objects and the senses.
If it is argued that suffering does not arise, [we reply: it is certainly not the case that there is no production of suffering.
Rather, it is the non-experience of suffering that occurs, for it is the arising of the cognition of suffering [that is absent].
Indeed, that which is not experienced as suffering and so forth cannot be the cause of affliction or benefit.

When pain, manifesting by its own nature, is itself suffering, then the cognition that takes it as its object is not [itself] suffering; therefore, this [rule] does not apply when the object and the feeling of the cognition are distinct.
Thus, for every cognition, there is a distinction between the object and the experience of it.

The similarity to the object is the objective support (ālambana), while the self is the cognition itself, manifest by its own nature. Furthermore, if there were no direct perception of the intellect, its apprehension would have to occur through an inferential mark (liṅga). And that [mark] could be either the sense organ, the object, the cognition, or even the preceding mental attention (manaskāra).

In this causal complex of the effect, no other capacity is observed for a related factor; therefore, the sense organ is not [the cause] due to deviation. Likewise, the object and the mental attention [are not the causes], for those two do not establish cognition.

That which is unestablished cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
