If it is held that the manifestation of the object is the mark, then surely that very manifestation is cognition; for by this [manifestation], the object is described as being manifested, since there can be no certainty regarding the manifestation of an object if that manifestation itself has not been experienced.
Now, if it is claimed that manifestation is merely some particularity (*viśeṣa*) of the object itself,
there is no particularity whatsoever in an object that is devoid of arising and passing away.
Or, if such a particularity were admitted, the consequence would follow that every moment the object undergoes destruction.
And that [object] may be either known or unknown; however, it is only when it is known that it can function as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
If it is not determined as "known," how can it be said that "this is known"?
Furthermore, even if it is not determined by its state of being known, how could it be a means of cognition?

Those who have not seen [an object] are never seen by another as "seers" anywhere; for that distinction exists even when there is seeing by another, and thus there would be the cognition of one's own [seeing]. Therefore, the inference of cognition does not depend upon its own specific property (*svadharma*).
Apart from the object-property itself, what property of its own could be distinct from the cognition itself?
That which is the cause of the cognition and arises from identical causes is perceived;
how then could there be a distinction of that [object] from the cognition? Furthermore, that which is born from other [causes] would be inconstant [with respect to the cognition].

Apart from the five objects such as form and so forth, the sense faculties, and the act of perception, no other effect of that [cognition] is observed. Among those, two are beyond the senses; not even one of the five objects is perceived [by itself].

That which is produced from the perception of a form, yet occurs otherwise through a separate possibility— such a thing, being unperceived in this way, is also an "inferential mark" (liṅga); this too is non-worldly (alaukika),
for one does not perceive that [mark] together with it even when the mark is present.
For how can a sign that is itself unperceived reveal [the object]? Precisely for that reason, if one describes its establishment prior to the sign,
then that [sign] too must be established by another example, resulting in an infinite regress.

Thus, the establishment of the object is through cognition; it is by no means from the object that [cognition is established], because if that [cognition] is not established, the object itself remains unestablished. Furthermore, having perceived direct perception as cognition, and having observed its desired designation and so forth—

Furthermore, there would be no inference of another's mind, because no connection [between that mind and a sign] has been observed in oneself; for the mark consisting of an object is not established in relation to mental cognition. Or else, how could one cognition be illuminated by another cognition according to your view?
How could there be a relationship of the manifested and the manifestor between two things whose nature is non-luminous?
How is an object manifested? Through the transfer of its form into the light. And that light, being of that very same nature, manifests itself by itself.
If it is accepted in that way, then cognition is established as self-cognizing within cognition;
otherwise, the object would likewise possess properties identical to those of the intellect.
Thus, for us, cognition, being of the nature of luminosity, manifests by itself.
Another cognition appears clearly within this [subsequent cognition] through the transition of its form;
for even when there is similarity, one cognition is not considered to be illuminated by another.
Because it illuminates itself, the object appears in that very form.
Just as in the case of two lamps, or a lamp and a jar,
the conventional usage of the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor is extended;
it is not by the mere presence of the object and the sense-faculty that the certainty [of perception] is established.
Therefore, since this [self-awareness] belongs to that [cognition], the perception of another must also be stated for it.

Furthermore, self-awareness is established even for memory; otherwise, if cognition were perceived by something else, there would be no apprehension of long vowels and the like, because many moments would not persist.
If [the cognition] were to remain stationary and without succession, then because it would appear all at once in the mind,
the phoneme would be non-successive and long. How could a phonemic part that lacks succession assist [another], while remaining unconnected with other phonemic parts?
Because it is perceived without sequence, cognition would likewise lack sequence,
as in the case of the final [sound]; and the sound, increasing from its previous state until the end,
would not perish on its own while remaining in its place, since there would be no difference [in its nature] even subsequently.
This same fault applies even if it is held that the phonemes exist simultaneously once they have arisen;
for, since they would arise from a single effort, subsequent efforts would be useless.
This fault attaches equally even if the phonemes are considered to be manifested.
If that [long sound] were grasped by multiple cognitions, then only the final cognition would be experienced;

that [final cognition] would not be a grasper of the long [sound], and thus there would be no memory of the cognition of the long [sound]. Furthermore, if the cognitions were perceived individually, then upon hearing that sound, [the sequence] would be heard as distinct.
There would be no appearance of continuity, and the synthesis [of moments] has already been refuted.
If one who hears [the sounds] as discrete still experiences the illusion of continuity,
then there would likewise be an illusion of continuity even when two short vowels are pronounced.
Furthermore, when the perception [of the object] has ceased, there can be no uninterrupted superimposition based on the sense organ;
for otherwise, it would follow that all cognitions from the senses are false.
Indeed, even the final phoneme itself lasts only as long as a blink of an eye.
And that [cognition] is established gradually through its connection with multiple atoms;
the time required for the passing of a single atom is considered the smallest unit of time, a *kṣaṇa*.
Since cognition is momentary, it apprehends the phonemes in succession.
Thus, regarding [the perception of] letters, forms, and so forth, every cognition— even if it appears as interrupted by another [cognition]— would be false in its object,
because the synthesis of entities occurs elsewhere than through sensory delusion.
Memory that is confused regarding the characteristic of difference is conceptual (*vikalpaka*). How could such [memory] have a clear manifestation when it is associated with verbal expression?
It has already been analyzed that there is no application of words to what is apprehended by the senses.
Even if one perceives [the object] as interrupted by the senses, if conceptual construction were to join it together,
then since the object and its cognition are constantly appearing,
how could it be "interrupted" when there is no subverting evidence and the logical principle remains intact?
If it is argued that this is due to the restriction of the capacities of cognitions, from what is that [restriction] held to arise?
If it is because cognitions are not observed to occur simultaneously, then that very point is what is being investigated:
would there be a restriction of their capacity only toward objects of the same class?
For indeed, conceptual constructions (vikalpas) arising in succession are correctly perceived as such;
by this, anyone who would imagine that recognition (pratyabhijñāna) regarding an object present before one is a direct perception (pratyakṣa) characterized by a clear manifestation is also refuted.
Since there is also a clear manifestation in the case of a mass of hair, a cluster of balls, a lamp-flame, and so forth,
how could perceptual cognition— despite the difference being well-known— be of such a nature? Therefore, the determination of the oneness of phonemes and the like does not arise from recognition.

Without the recollection of what was previously experienced and the superimposition of its properties, there can be no cognition that "this is that very same thing"; and how could such a cognition arise from the senses?
Furthermore, it is not possible for the cognition of the object and the awareness of that cognition to occur simultaneously.
Two appearances are perceived, yet the object and the cognition of the object do not appear separately;

for there is no such thing as a cognition appearing as an object while the external object exists in isolation. Otherwise, if they were grasped as having a single form, it would follow that there is no distinction between them.

If the object and the cognition of the object— which are not perceived as distinct in consciousness due to their lack of clearly discernible difference— are later remembered separately, how could that be so?
Even if experience arises sequentially for the object and the mind, this [distinction] remains unaccounted for.
The fault of the objection regarding the multiplicity of appearances is difficult to remove.
First, there is the cognition of the object; from that, there is the cognition of the appearance of the object.
For a pure cognition [devoid of an image] could not be the cognition of an object.

For indeed, a single form such as blue and a single act of cognition are perceived; however, in the cognition that appears as blue, no further cognition is observed. If there were an experience [of that cognition] by another cognition, there would likewise have to be a memory of it.
By what means is that [object] perceived? If it is by another cognition, then who produces this continuous chain for those who possess knowledge?
If it is the preceding cognition itself, there would be no transition to another object.

Without grasping that preceding cognition— which has attained the status of being an object, which is proximate, which is productive, and which is fixed in its own nature of generating a cognition— how could a subsequent cognition grasp another [object]? Furthermore, that [preceding cognition] is restricted to its own nature in the production of knowledge within itself.
Who indeed could obstruct an internal [cognition] with something external?
For even if an external object is present, it is not capable of obstructing that [cognition];
otherwise, no one would ever experience cognition while an object is in its proximity.

And since there is no state whatsoever in which an object is present, the root of cognition is destroyed; thus, even memory is destroyed—this is the clear conclusion. For those conceptualizations of the past and so forth, there is no proximity of an object.
Because there is no cause for its transition,
the cognition of an object would perish gradually through the exhaustion of the capacity to produce knowledge within the self;
if there were a transition to another object, from where would that very cognition of the [previous] object arise?

When the capacity of the preceding cognition is exhausted, there is no subsequent cognition, for without the preceding cognition, [the subsequent one] does not arise; this is because when a cognition is impaired by attachment to another object, the arising of [another] cognition is not observed. Even when cognitions of different types arise simultaneously, it is due to one [cognition] being more powerful.
Because of the impairment instilled by the [preceding] mind, there can be no arising from anything other than the *ālaya*.
Otherwise, a subsequent mental state would not depend on the similarity of the preceding mental activity;
thus, the sequential arising of mental cognitions must be established as being dependent [on a causal substratum].

If, because the mind is unitary, it cannot reach another object when it is attached to one, and thus another cognition does not arise— [we reply that] this would never happen, since cognitions arise simultaneously; and if [the mind] were functioning equally toward all objects, there would always be a reaching of other objects due to that equality.
And for those [cognitions] arising merely from the conjunction of the self and the mind, birth [of cognition] would occur all at once.
If the action were indeed one, how could there be many perceptions?
Even if it were gradual, it would not be capable [of producing them], since there would be no difference [in its state] even subsequently.

By this, the body and the person are said to be [the causes]; if the restriction [of cognition] is due to mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), from what does that [impression] arise? If it is argued that it arises subsequently from cognition, let it be as you agree.
There is no "objectivity" other than being produced; being produced is the very definition of being an object.
Indeed, there is no light that is ungraspable, nor is there such a thing in that which is partless, such as subtlety and the like.
There would be a loss of the power of being grasped for nothing other than that which has the nature of producing [a cognition].
For, in the definition of the graspable, production is certainly not something other than the state of being grasped.
For otherwise, form and the rest would not be direct contributors to cognition.
What other restriction of its existence [to that object] could there be for them than the definition of being apprehended?
Since that [definition] also applies to cognition, it too is established as being grounded in reality.
The perception of the object and the appropriation [of the sense-faculties] is the characteristic of the object for the mind; likewise,
for those of impure intellect, this reflection on the characteristic of the object regarding form and so forth, as well as the mind itself, is the inconceivable domain of the yogins.
In that case, by becoming subtle and so forth, the object of perception would reach a state of non-perceptibility.
What has arisen in the cognition of form and the rest such that it did not exist previously?
Therefore, since the apprehension of its own cognition exists, that alone is the immediate cause.
That very [cognition] is the object of the mind; therefore, there is no apprehension of an external object distinct from it.

Even in the absence of multiple or single powers, an entity produces multiple or single effects by its very nature (prakṛti); thus it has been declared. If it were not so, [the effect] would not arise from the multiple or the single.
Nothing arises from a single cause; rather, everything arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
It has been stated that even a single [effect] may arise from two complexes, and thus it is produced by many.
If a subsequent cognition were to apprehend both the object and the preceding cognition, [it would follow that the latter is perceived].
Because it would manifest both prior and posterior objects within a single moment of thought at the beginning of reflection,
two verbal expressions would necessarily appear simultaneously— both seen in succession and without succession—
and each object would appear twice, because of the manifestation of both the self and that which knows it.

If, during the transition to another object, the final [cognition] is not experienced, then it follows that all cognitions would be unexperienced, just like the experience of another. If [it is argued that] what is experienced by the self is perception, yet it is not experienced by others; [then the same consequence follows].
That self-experience is established; it is for this reason that it is so stated. For one who desires the manifested through manifestation, there would be no proof of the cause of manifestation.
If the world were manifested even when manifestation itself is unestablished, then this entire world would be manifested.

Some maintain that because the other person is the one to be convinced, even if [the reason] has not been seen by oneself, it is a means of proof provided it has been seen by others; the statement "seen by oneself" is intended to reject this view. However, this is not accepted regarding the object of inference, because only what has been examined is admitted as a valid basis.

For in this case, no inference proceeds to invalidate the authority of the word (*vāk*), since the proof (*sādhana*) has been stated for the sake of another. At that time, that [inference] is not a means of valid cognition; it is unestablished, and therefore everything established by it is likewise unestablished.
If [the property] is established for one who possesses that scripture, then whose is the scripture?
How can that which is sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) be established as scripture?
And how could there be an acceptance of something contradictory to it by that very same person?
If one accepts something other than that [scripture], then that member of the proof [the scripture] would lack authority.
Why is that? For what reason was it not stated as a means of proof—that from which one's own realization arises?
By whatever reasoning scripture is to be accepted, why is that same reasoning not also the means of grasping this [realization]?
For one who exists as a natural being, those means by which the prior occurrence of cognition and the senses were established are sufficient for this person’s knowledge of the capacity of objects;
likewise, those things whose continuity is severed and which are not within the range even of a universal [concept] [are also known].
In those objects, there is no consideration whatsoever of the probandum or the probans;
for when the determination of reality or unreality occurs by virtue of human intention,
both the valid reason and its fallacy are set aside, since they do not depend upon the actual nature of the thing.

An existent object depends upon cognition, whereas a non-existent one cannot be established by cognition. Even for that which exists, a cognition that is not connected to the actual thing is equivalent to no cognition at all.
[The means of proof are] the logical mark (*liṅga*), which is either an essential nature (*svabhāva*), an effect (*kārya*), or the non-perception of what is perceptible (*dṛśyādarśana*).
If [the reason] is established as being connected with the thing in reality, how can it be unestablished for oneself?
It is improper for another to go from one point to another by means of what is imagined by the opponent;
rather, a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) proceeds from the connection between two things to eliminate the other in the absence of one.

The inclusion of the term "object" (artha) is for the purpose of establishing that those things whose nature is superimposed by verbal conceptualization (*kalpanā*) lack the status of being a logical mark (*aliṅgatva*), because an object is established only through another object [in reality],
whereas conceptualization and scripture follow merely the whim of the author.

Because a real entity cannot exist otherwise [than as it is], conceptual constructions are deviant. Since the understanding of an object arises from the object itself, the capacity of the statement of the thesis and the reason resides in the object; therefore, their status as means of proof does not exist intrinsically.

That statement of the thesis is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for communicating the speaker’s intention; however, because doubt arises from it, it is not a direct proof (*sādhana*) of the probandum (*sādhya*). Even by virtue of expressing the probandum itself, it is not sufficient as an indirect proof either.
The statement of a reason, though itself incapable [of proving the conclusion], indicates that which is capable;
it is called "incapable" because its object is the meaning of the reason.
If it is argued that this statement of the reason is indeed capable because it prompts the application [of the reason].
For one who desires to know due to doubt regarding that [reason], there would be reliance on a formal treatise (*prakaraṇa*);
since this same [reliance] applies equally even when accepting the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there would be an infinite regress.
However, the internal capacity (*antaraṅga-sāmarthya*) resides in the three characteristics (*tri-rūpa*).
In that case, the application of memory is established just like [the application of] that [word];
for if the object has not been made known, the operation of the reason is impossible.
If it is argued that its capacity is established solely by the making known of the object, [we reply:]...
Even without this [explicit statement], when it is stated that "whatever is produced is like this—
all such things are impermanent," the cognition of its destruction would arise by implication.
This is because the proof of the subject (pakṣa) is not obstructed even if it is not explicitly mentioned.

The failure to state any one of the three [factors] is declared to be a deficiency (*nyūnatā*). Alternatively, if he states the thesis (*pratijñā*) as the expression of the probandum (*sādhya*), he is not subject to faults,
because the discussion is restricted solely to the means of proof (*sādhana*), given that fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) would otherwise follow.
Even a statement made without qualification brings about doubt regarding that which belongs to a single class;
otherwise, it would follow that every statement of a probandum would constitute a thesis (*pratijñā*).
If it is argued that this does not apply to the opponent because a statement of what is already established serves as a means of proof (*sādhana*), then [the same logic] applies here as well.

Now, how can the statement of the thesis (*sādhya-nirdeśa*) be a member of the proof (*sādhana-avayava*)? Such mockery—consisting of the introduction of fallacious arguments and the like, followed by refutations—is irrelevant; for it has been indicated that this is not the correct method (*nyāya*).
Even though the meaning is already understood, the definition is stated for the sake of avoiding confusion;
that [definition] has four characteristics, established by the words *rūpa*, *nipāta*, *iṣṭa*, and *svayam*.
It includes what is unestablished (*asiddha*), what is not a means of proof (*asādhana*), what is merely stated (*artha-ukta*), and the proponent's own admission (*vādy-abhyupagama*).

Even if not explicitly stated, that which is pervaded by [the proponent's] intention is considered the probandum (*sādhya*), just as in the case of one's own purpose (*ātma-artha*). Although all other desired [conclusions] are excluded, the exclusion of grounds for doubt is expressed in the commentary (*vṛtti*) through the explicit mention of "himself" (*svayam*); and this [mention] was made for that very purpose.
The distinction between the property and the subject is said to arise from their mutual dependence;
even if it is not explicitly stated, its understanding may occur through the context of what is intended.
Furthermore, the fault of "lack of concomitance" (*ananvaya*) in the example is as previously described.
If [the opponent claims] that the self is something other [than the body], then since that [otherness] is unestablished, it would contradict what is intended [by the proponent].
If the probans which was not put forward in the debate is not proven, then what is there to be proven? Otherwise, it would either result in an unintended consequence or in total futility.

In arguments for [the self] being accompanied by a second [entity], there is the fault of being either "without a basis" (*niranvaya*) or "contradictory" (*viruddha*). This has already been stated. Now, if it is argued that the probandum (*sādhya*) is intended in its general sense, then because there is no other object [corresponding to that generality], it is not established when the body is not attained.
This is merely the delirious prattle of those who speak while empty-headed; it is a thought born of dullness.

Even if destruction were identical [to sound], such a conceptualization—distinguishing between sound and a jar—is not established, because sound is proven by means of its destruction which is already established.

Likewise, if there were the existence of a different entity, then the pot would also possess that [impermanence]. If it is argued that impermanence does not follow as qualified by sound, that is not so, because it excludes non-connection.
For exclusion (vyavaccheda) is of two kinds: the exclusion of non-connection and the exclusion of connection with another.
But if [the reason] is excluded from non-connection, there is no lack of positive concomitance (ananvaya) with another;
that very universal is what is to be proven, and it is not a case of proving what is already established.
And that [universal], as qualified by the subject (dharmin), does not suffer from the fault of lacking positive concomitance (niranvaya).

By this, the property and the substratum as qualified by [the other] are refuted; for one who denies them does not thereby invalidate the substratum itself, since it is not the means of proof in that way. Indeed, a denial of the aggregate is not contradictory with respect to the substratum alone.
Because that [subject] is not intended in such a way as to be the probandum; here, only the property (*dharma*) is the probandum.

Even though many properties may reside in a single subject (*dharmin*) according to various treatises, the probandum must be intended by [the proponent] himself; thus, the word "himself" (*svayaṃ*) is employed.

Because of the very acceptance of the treatise (*śāstra*), everything [contained therein] is included; therefore, if there is a sublation [of the thesis], even a single [point] therein would constitute a fault, whether it pertains to the reason (*hetu*) or the proposition (*pratijñā*).
For example, when the perishability of sound is being established, there would be a fault because the quality of smell as a property of earth (*bhū-guṇatā*) is impaired.

If it is argued that the reason is not contradictory because the subject (*prakṛti*) is not under discussion, then that same [lack of relevance] applies elsewhere as well. If, on the other hand, the subject is indeed under discussion here, then there is a contradiction with the meaning of the treatise (*śāstrārthabādha*).
Alternatively, one might claim that [the subject] is intended by the proponent through the means of proof consisting of the properties of the subject and so forth.
Through certain contexts, a desire may arise and is understood by them;
yet to say forcibly, "This is your desire," is clearly the work of a Lord (Īśvara),
for one who speaks thus is contradicted by the fallibility of that [desire] which has the effect as its logical mark.
And when a matter that is not invariably concomitant is sublated, what harm is done to the other?
Furthermore, it has been stated that inference does not depend upon scripture regarding its own object;
therefore, when that [object] is established, it is well-established, and at that time the treatise is not taken into account.

If it were argued that there would then be an abandonment of the thesis, that is not so, because [the thesis] was not accepted [as a premise]. For this [scripture] is merely a means for what is to be accepted; even though it exists at that time, it is not a constituent part [of the proof]. Thus, when the two objects of cognition are purified, one may adopt a treatise.

For that would indeed be the time for one who intends to act; at that time, there is sublation by the treatise (*śāstra*). Because reflection [based on] that [treatise] is incompatible with what is established by it, it is not applicable to objects already proven. When there is a transition to the third stage, the adoption of the treatise is the logical rule (*nyāya*).

In that case as well, only the sublation of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) when it is connected [to the subject] is to be avoided, and not the sublation of other [properties], because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of infinite regress. By whom was this rule established that "in all investigations, the treatise (śāstra) must be accepted"?

Now, fire cannot be apprehended by means of smoke for those who hold unestablished tenets. Alas, by whom have these treacherous graspings of tenets been bestowed upon a person born empty, who perceives neither merit nor fault?

If a proof were required to demonstrate the entirety of a treatise within a single example, then that would be a superhuman standard. For what is not established when an unrelated property remains unestablished?

If the reason stated for the sake of proving that [property] is indeed defective, how can it be established therein? For people infer consciousness, fire, and so forth from speech, smoke, and so on, even without having brought all the properties of the subject into the example.
When an object establishes its own nature (*svabhāva*) or its cause (*kāraṇa*) without deviation,

it does not cease from its nature even when there is a contradiction with someone's thesis. And another person, while undertaking that [object], [encounters] what is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) with their desired [conclusions].

How can that reason (hetu), which has the property to be proven (sādhya) as its object, fail to establish it? If it is argued that even if the reason is not explicitly stated, it is still [a valid] reason, then what contradiction is there for the proponent here? For the invalidation of the treatise (śāstra-bādhana) does not arise through a defect in his verbal expression.

If it is argued that there is a fault because of the statement of a sublation (*bādhaka*), [we reply: if he did not state it, would he not have sublated [the opponent's position]? Since he does nothing at all, why is he considered faulty?
This is unlike other fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), where one's own intended [thesis] is simply not established.
One would be at fault for stating something useless, because that [useless thing] is not being established here.
If something in a certain treatise is illogical, it is refuted;
yet one may state another thing that is logical—such is the practice of the royal court.
If one were to treat all objects as identical, it would be impossible to state a means of proof (sādhana).
Consequently, since [the distinction between object and subject] would be destroyed everywhere, this established relationship between the probandum (sādhya) and the proof (sādhana) would collapse.
Let there be sublation (bādhana), for two contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single locus (dharmin).
In this case, there is contradiction by way of being contradictory and certain;
even though those two stand in a relationship of neither the sublated nor the sublator, [contradiction occurs] because of the subversion of the meaning of the treatise.
If there were sublation even in the absence of a connection, then everything would be the sublator of everything.
If it is argued that there is a connection because [the reason] is sublated only in that [case], then no,
for every reason must be examined for its merits and defects regarding its own probandum;
the connection here is not seen in the sense of being necessarily concomitant (*nāntarīyakatā*) with the probandum.

If [it is argued that] only the contradiction with scripture (*śāstra*) is a fault here, then that [fault] is equal when [the argument] is made by another. If everything perceived in the scripture were to be proven because of the acceptance of the scripture,
it would follow that the thesis, the example, and the reason are unestablished.

If it is argued that because they are stated as means of proof (*sādhana*), [the thesis] is not so, we reply: since it is what is desired to be expressed, the status of being the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is established by logic—is not revoked by mere verbal statement. If it were the case that what is not desired by the proponent is not the probandum, then anything else not desired by him would likewise not be the probandum.

If a property (*dharma*) is unprovable, then how can that which subverts the unprovable be contradictory? If the meaning [of the thesis] lies outside the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*), then the word "himself" (*svayam*) is also redundant. If it is for the sake of engaging with one's own desire regarding the treatises (*śāstra*), from where would such a doubt arise?
If he is not contradicted by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), who can prevent him from accepting [a position]?
If he is contradicted by a means of valid cognition, who can urge him to speak?
Previously, too, he accepted his own philosophical tenet solely according to his own will.

How could he possibly obtain another [means of proof] at all? Here, demonstrating that [the opponent's position] would result in the destruction of what is accepted, the impossibility of proof, and infinite regress, [the author] himself cited the scripture regarding the various conflicting views on perception.
In order to exclude a subject (*dharmin*) that is differentiated by conventional consensus (*samaya*),

another [teacher] stated the word "itself" (*svayam*) for the purpose of grasping a well-known subject. Since the investigation has already been introduced, the locus (*āśraya*) is established as being well-known.
Since there is no dispute regarding the categories of objects whose distinctions are imagined according to one's own whim,

[the opponent] then asserts that [the subject] is not something to be proven because it is already established by the very designation of the locus (*dharmin*). This point is already covered by the rule that [the subject] must be indicated by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone.
For if it were possible to state [the probandum] by way of its being already established,
then stating it solely as something yet to be proven would be fruitful; furthermore, it has been described that the object of inference is a universal (*sāmānya*).

In this case, even if it were not stated in such a way, nothing would be contradicted regarding the subject (*pakṣa*). If one were to make the property-bearer (*dharmin*) itself the probandum (*sādhya*), what of it? That [fault] cannot [arise].
Why? Because of the absence of the logical reason’s (*hetu*) positive concomitance (*anvaya*); nor is this fault present in those two [the reason and the example].
A defect that depends upon a subsequent member [of the syllogism] is not accepted as a defect of the thesis (*pakṣa*);

likewise, it would follow that a defect of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth would also be a defect of the thesis, because the thesis is sublated by all [the members]. Therefore, [a defect of the thesis] belongs only to that which is indicated by the thesis alone.

No other faults of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) are recognized, except for those that contradict perception and so forth. Apart from what is sublated by the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and the rest, the definition of the thesis is stated for the purpose of excluding under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*vyatireka*).
The mention of the word "itself" (svayam) serves to exclude [the cases of] particles, nouns, and verbs;

the mention of "intended" (iṣṭa), when not negated by the word "together with" (saha), excludes under-extension. The definition of the thesis (pakṣa) is the acceptance of what is to be proven; therefore, those [cases] do not constitute a thesis.
When [an alternative] is rejected because it is sublated, and when [the term] applies to the remainder because it lacks the defining characteristic;
when the restrictive sense is already understood through the expression of what is intended by oneself;
and because of its connection with a word ending in a kṛtya suffix—[the particle *eva*] is stated for the purpose of excluding another time.

In this context, the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *iṣ* (to desire) is not a constituent part [of the compound]; therefore, in the word *īpsita*, it is indeed a constituent part. Likewise, unestablished reasons (*asiddha-hetu*) and so forth are excluded. Furthermore, because they are non-expressive, it is improper; thus, [the object] is desired by oneself through one's own [will].
Without depending on the entirety of a treatise, that which is intended [by the proponent] is what is to be proven (sādhya).
Therefore, even when something desired is sublated by being mixed with what is not intended,
the thesis (pakṣa) and the reason (hetu) are not defective, provided the intended object of proof remains unsublated.
And that acceptance is held to be uncontradicted by the two means of valid cognition.
Because a reason is stated regarding what is doubtful, that which is excluded is not a locus for the reason.
Through the divisions of inference, that sublation is said to be fourfold.
In that regard, the means [of knowledge] consists of the member of logical necessity (*kārya-aṅga*), the member of essential nature (*svabhāva-aṅga*), and the stability of the world;

the authoritative person (*āpta*) is one who intends to refrain from harming others and whose speech is endowed with certainty regarding reality. Thus, his own word and the treatise (*śāstra*) are said to be equal.
Just as speech does not operate when the self lacks authority, so too there is no inquiry into an object perceived through scripture if that [self] is not its basis.
For if it were the basis for the introduction of that [inquiry], then scripture would be the sublater. This is the point.

In order to express its meaning through its own words, it is mentioned together with that [other] for the sake of perceiving their similarity; likewise, an example has been described here that corresponds to it,
because in the absence of valid means of cognition (pramāṇas), the words of the treatise would be untenable.

In the case of contradiction with one's own words, there is a clear example in scripture: "The dharma taught by the Teacher brings happiness after death. However, this is merely shown as an illustration; for even in the case of a teacher, when there is a contradictory statement regarding a factual matter that does not depend on such [scriptural authority], [the fault remains].

There can be no sublation or obstruction between two [statements] because they possess equal status; just as it is with one's own words, so too is that [statement] of his [the opponent] essentially his own word. Of those two, whichever possesses validity shall be the sublater of the other.
Otherwise, how could a thesis or an inference— lacking logical support and being of equal status or consistent with reality— subvert [the opponent's position]? Furthermore,
the authority of scriptures has already been refuted.
Therefore, this fault is admitted in the case of investigations concerning accepted tenets (*abhyupāya*).

Consequently, although accepted tenets are not outside the scope of inference, they are treated separately in order to demonstrate the distinction between their objects. This is because [the tenet] acts as a sublation [of other positions].

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), or the separate formulation [of the thesis] would be purposeless; for if difference were merely a matter of words, there would be an obstacle even to one's own statement.
Therefore, because it is accepted [as authoritative], a treatise (*śāstra*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding all things.
If one does not accept a sublater, what indeed could that sublater be?

There would be no distinction between contradiction with one's own words and contradiction with one's own words and treatises. Furthermore, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is established entirely by the will of the person [who asserts it].

Therefore, there is no harm in disregarding the treatises regarding matters that are well-established; however, if one rejects the authority of scripture concerning things that are beyond perception, no inquiry whatsoever can proceed.
Even the investigation that primarily consists in pointing out contradictions applies only to such cases, as follows:

Passion and the like are the root of unrighteousness, while bathing is the purification of unrighteousness; that scripture which is not contradicted by established reasoning or its own words regarding both the seen and the unseen— that is to be accepted— such is the reflection that proceeds.

Since the designation of desired objects by words follows human intention and is not prohibited with respect to those objects, the person whose speech is unimpaired is here called an "authority" (*āpta*). That which is produced from such linguistic convention is what is referred to by the term "dharma."
By the metaphorical attribution of the term "means of valid cognition" (*māna*) to perception and the rest,

it is indicated that the entire universe— whether things already produced or yet to be produced— is by its very nature suitable for those [cognitions] which arise based upon them, because they function according to desire and do not exclude [their objects].
Whether it is yet to come or has already occurred, that which conforms to the mere object [of cognition] sublates [the contrary],
for one who obstructs it by means of that verbal fitness;
indeed, by the power of that very fitness, the sound is established as a reality.
Since everything [is established] by this [perception], even when that [object] is not perceived, its establishment follows from that;

otherwise, there would be no "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatā) for the reason that sublates [the object]. Therefore, the negation of that [object] must occur through inference, because the word's meaning does not function within the domain of the senses.

The uncommon nature of reasons occurs where there is no positive concomitance; this is considered the result of the very formulation of a reason. Words depend upon conventions, and those conventions depend solely upon intention.

"There is no non-establishment of things established by verbal testimony"—this is a statement based on what is established by verbal testimony. It demonstrates the absence of the "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) in cases to be proven by inference; therefore, inference proceeds from such cognition.
Alternatively, when people speak [of perception], they say that inference is non-existent;
yet what is the point of that, since cognition has an object distinct from inference?
Therefore, because of inference, there is the conformity to the existence or non-existence of things.
It has been indicated that the application [of a term] to a distinct object occurs by virtue of that [intention], for it arises from desire;
thus, one who does not accept the moon-nature of the hare-marked one—what cognition could he possibly desire?
Therefore, with respect to him, that [reason] is considered non-common (asādhāraṇa) because there is no corroborating example.
This is not stated solely with reference to this specific example, because it is a general definition; for likewise, if one says "the *dhātrī* tree is not a tree," that statement is contradicted,
since in common worldly usage, camphor, silver, and so forth are also seen [to be called trees].
If [the reason] exists by virtue of convention, what is its "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatā) such that it is called [a fallacy]?
If it were established in some [subject], then that would be established by the force of the thing itself (*vastubalena*).
If one accepts that it is established through cognition, then there is no way to exclude it even in the case of [proving] that the moon is not the moon.
Since that [conceptual content] is established with respect to the object, it cannot be excluded even in the case of the moon;
yet, if that object is absent, there is no fault even if it is excluded in the case of the moon.
Therefore, for those words which arise from conventions restricted to non-entities (avastu), [there is no contradiction].

Objects are fit for properties because there is no obstruction to one's desire [to designate them]. An inference whose object is fitness, known as "cognition" (*pratīta*), refutes that which obstructs such fitness, arising from the non-denial of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).
By the statement that "there is no restriction of meaning for words that follow convention," the denial of these [words] is contradicted here;
[for they refer] either to the object of a causal designation or to an ultimate object.
One who denies words is not contradicted by that [denial], as it has been described. Therefore, in order to demonstrate the difference in their objects,
even cognition— which is not external to inference— is treated separately, just as before.
Demonstrating the purpose for explaining the two established [means of knowledge] separately,
he stated that these two— [inference and perception]— are accompanied by their respective causes, and not for the sake of subverting inference or perception.
Even in that case, regarding the subversion by perception, [it occurs] because sound possesses a manifold nature.

Whatever form of the well-known [object] appears in scripture is non-dual, because no cognition arises that perceives a variegated appearance. Therefore, the statement regarding that object is sublated by direct perception when it is negated.
That very form is the object there; the remainder is characterized by exclusion (vyāvṛtti). Being of the nature of a non-entity, the universal is therefore not within the range of the senses.
Thus, it is established that universal properties are not objects of direct perception.
It has been revealed by the statement "it is audible" that there is no sublation even in the case of a negation;
for, since [the object] is in every way of an inexpressible nature, it is established as such, and based upon that,
the object of the senses is said to be sublated by the force of that [inexpressibility].
In all cases, that property which the proponent intends to establish for himself is the subject;

there may be sublation (bādhā) regarding that property-possessor (dharmin), but not regarding another property within that same dharmin. Otherwise, what obstruction would there be if another dharmin were sublated?

Since the meaning is already established by this definition, the mention of "its own property" (svadharma) is repeated [in the definition of the thesis] so that it may be clearly understood that if there is a sublation of the property,
there must also be a sublation of the locus (dharmin).
This is because the locus, being the substratum, is contradicted when that which depends upon it is contradicted.

Otherwise, because of the statement that "such a property (dharma) is the probandum," one would consider the mention of the subject (sva-dharmin) to be intended solely for the purpose of excluding that [other property]. Now, is this not also established by implication? True; however, some [proponents] hold that the subject...
Even when [the reason] is restricted to the subject alone, they have fallen into fallacy.

For example, when it is stated: "Space and so forth are not produced by others because they are not the cause of sound and so forth at once, and because they do not possess a prior form," the opponent replies:
In the same way, even if the subject (*dharmin*)— such as space (*vyoman*) and so forth— is non-existent by its very nature,
there is no subversion of the intended probandum (*sādhya*) anywhere;
for when both [the subject and the property] are to be proven, that which obstructs the property to be proven [does not apply].
The sublation of the subject (*dharmin*) therein is described by the term "sublation" (*bādhā*).
Likewise, since the subject here is also what is to be proven (*sādhya*), [the sublation] does not apply to the subject in isolation.
If this were the case, there would be no sublation here, for [the subject] does not possess a capacity that could be produced by anything else.

04145 Because sound and so forth are not causes [of pleasure] all at once, pleasure and so forth [are momentary], as before; 04146 here, if the reason were conclusive, there would be contradiction. [But it is not,] because successive action and impermanence are not contradictory in the counter-example (vipakṣa).

Because there is doubt regarding its exclusion, this [reason] is held to be a "residual" (śeṣavat) type of difference. Since the property (dharma) that one intends for oneself is the probandum (sādhya), it is indicated that its locus must be what is sublated, and not something isolated or residing in another locus.
It is stated that by the scripture itself, there is either the sublation or the non-sublation of the properties of another;
likewise, it is stated that by means of its own property-bearer (*dharmin*), there is also [the sublation or non-sublation] of another property-bearer.
By every defect in the proof (*sādhana*), the very thesis (*pakṣa*) is obstructed.
Nevertheless, that which is designated merely as a "proposition" (pratijñā) possesses the status of being a flaw of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).
A flaw that depends upon subsequent members [of the syllogism] is what is bound to it;
therefore, it has been stated that [flaws such as] an unestablished locus (*asiddhāśraya*) and so forth are not flaws of the thesis.

By this very [method], the sublation of the subject (dharmin), of the properties (dharma), of their specific qualities, and of the nature of the subject itself— which constitute the essential parts of the probandum— is demonstrated. To illustrate that,
a mere direction is stated for the sake of perceiving the meaning.

There exists another entity, distinct from the characteristics of substance, which is perceived in conjunction [with it]. A thesis concerning that which is invisible and undifferentiated is purposeless;
for the whole (avayavin) is accepted as the effect, which is impossible among things that are invisible.
And if another [entity] that is indistinguishable [from the substance] were to be proven [as its cause], it would be a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
If gravity and downward motion were to exist [in the substance], there would be a depression of the scale;
therefore, that [substance] is devoid of quality and action, and thus is not an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
For that very reason, this [substance] is not visible, because its effect and form are unperceived;
for there is no other specific quality that necessarily follows which could sublate that [non-perception].
From the subtlest [particle] up to the gross substance, they are identical in nature, like the falling of a thread of light.
Another has said that there is no motion of the gravity of a separate substance;
for if a heap of dust were joined to [a scale] gradually on one hand and all at once on the other,
there would be a difference in its weight when weighed separately and together.
It is not logical that there should be equality in number for the *māṣaka* and other weights in sequence,
from a single mustard seed up to a great heap, if their increasing weight were not perceived through weighing.

The weight [of a substance] down to that of a mustard seed is difficult to perceive, yet it is not insignificant; its cause is its own weight, because the weight of the effect is not perceived. But surely, like a ray of light, that object is unseen, and its effect is not observed.
04161 Just as with weight and non-motion, because all those qualities are not perceived, 04162 there is no increase in the māṣaka and so forth; that [non-perception] is the indicator.
04162 Just as when form and so on are not seen by their respective sense organs, even though they have increased further and further.
However, because there is the possibility of contradiction by one's own words and so forth,
another example may also be understood through the direction already stated.
But because actions have the three times as their object, that which is not of such a nature [is not a valid action].

Likewise, even when the probandum (sādhya) has been explicitly set forth for the opponent, it is not [then] "intended" (iṣṭa); however, within the context of the demonstration [of the thesis], the term "probandum" includes everything that is not yet established. Therefore, the mention of the "probandum" does not depend upon a specific qualification such as "intended."
Therefore, he has provided an example of a reason and an illustration that are unestablished;

otherwise, even in the case of things like a hare's horn—which are entirely unestablished—there would be the status of being a probandum, since everything would be unestablished in some respect. Thus, his position is not tenable.
Regarding the analysis of the introduction and refutation of distinctions such as those of karma:
[the objection that] "because its nature was previously unestablished, it is a member of the thesis" is incorrect;
for those [distinctions] are of equal status as established tenets, since they are characterized by [one's own] acceptance.

Even if the collection [of the subject and the property] is what is to be proven (*sādhya*), each of the two would then be mutually a qualifier; thus, the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be unestablished. If it is maintained that the word "to be proven" (*sādhya*) applies only to the locus (*dharmin*) because [otherwise] it is impossible [for the whole to be the object], [the following objection follows].
Enough with the treatise; let the world proceed as appropriate.

Through the power of the statement of the means (*sādhana*), the status of being the probandum (*sādhyatā*) is attained for that object. Furthermore, because it is pervaded by the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, the means of proof is beyond suspicion.
Since the restriction [of the reason] is already established by that [invariable concomitance], the statement of the definition of the thesis is redundant;
for that statement results in pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is understood through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*).
Furthermore, contradiction (*viruddhatā*) consists in the non-connection with what is intended, as well as non-assistance and non-coexistence.
In this way, all defects of the members [of a syllogism] would become defects of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Furthermore, it has been established that a defect of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) does not depend upon anything else;
thus, that very [defect], being impossible in what is intended and unestablished, is refuted.
If [the proponent] were to proclaim that sound itself possesses impermanence and its cause in this manner,

what else would there be here to illustrate the example other than the demonstration of the actual state of affairs? When one has stated a specific instance and then proceeds to apply it to the universal, [the example is established].
"Is there no fruit in its pervasion by that [universal], or rather, what is the point of following after a universal?
Since the negation [of the probandum] occurs precisely while one remains within the word itself, he therefore spoke thus:
by speaking of another object that is contradictory, he declares the distinctness of the heard [word]."
And that [exclusion] does not exist for universals because their differentiation is not rejected,
just as in a certain context one might say, "A tree is not a *śiṃśapā* alone. By that much, there would be no negation of the application of the term "all" to a single instance.
Because of the distinction between the object to be known and the means of knowing, the probans— which is to become the property of the subject—
is unestablished; thus, its status as a means of knowledge is unestablished with respect to the subject itself in its own proof,
since the distinction between property and subject is not established in all entities.

If it is argued that the fault is equal everywhere, we say no; for there is a distinction made from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). In investigations into ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), identity and difference are denied in respect to things that are conventionally established.

This established convention regarding the objects of inference and the act of inferring is postulated by relying upon a distinction that is thoroughly proven by cognition; for the discerning person, within cognitions that are each grounded in their own respective distinctions.

The substratum (dharmin) and its properties (dharmas) appear; linguistic convention (vyavahāra) is based upon them. Here, that very [substratum], brought forward by convention and perceived as devoid of distinctness, is the probandum (sādhya). When it is led to the state of being a means of proof (sādhana), it is thereby revealed as unestablished (asiddha).
Because there is a difference in properties between the particular and the universal, there exists a relationship of part and whole;
thus, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it arises from effort.
Even though [the property] is a part of the subject (*pakṣa*), it is not unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to a different locus (*dharmī*), because it is not contradicted.

Just as a horse is not [inferred] to possess horns simply because it is horned, so too this lump [of clay] does not [possess horns]. Furthermore, the exclusion [of the counter-example] is not a constituent part of the time of the probandum; for even if one observes that exclusion, a specific property cannot be the object of the thesis, since there is a distinction between the properties [of the example and the subject].
In order to facilitate easy comprehension through the various classifications of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*),

a concise summary of the meaning of the section on logical reasons (*hetu*) is stated [in the following] sūtras: [the reason excludes] non-connection [with the subject], connection with others [similar instances], and absolute non-connection [with dissimilar instances].
The particle *eva*, which functions as an exclusionary, distinguishes the property (*dharma*) when it is uttered together with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), a qualified (*viśeṣya*), or a verb (*kriyā*).
Even when it is employed according to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), this is the meaning understood from it.

A sentence has exclusion as its result, as in the cases: "Caitra is an archer," "Pārtha is an archer," or "The lotus is blue"; for even in these instances, the exclusion of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi-vyavaccheda*) is understood regarding the objects.
Because it is thus established by convention, by implication, and because the sound [of the word] follows the speaker's intention,

the qualification of the subject (dharmin) and the property (dharma) serves to exclude non-connection with that [property]. Thus, the property, being qualified by that, does not incur the fault of lacking a logical connection (niranvaya).

For the sake of establishing essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*), there are two types of reasons and their two respective contraries. Because of dispute regarding particulars and universals, the remaining [reasons] are those that establish through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
For the pervasion of what is to be understood by a cause is not established by anything other than its own nature.
Because deviation is possible, the result [of the reason] functions in two ways; therefore,
cognition immediately following effort does not necessarily belong to something that already exists,
since its operation is entirely useless in the case of the covering, the sense organ, and the word.
Since that which is independent [of other causes] could never produce an effect due to the contradiction with its nature as a cause,
it is established that such knowledge— which has an occasional result— is the logical mark (*liṅga*) for [proving] that [omniscience].
By this very [reasoning], although the essential nature [of the omniscient being] is already well-known, it is treated separately.
When the probans is stated together with the effect, let it not be thought that everything is like this;

for the statement of the reason is made for the sake of etymological derivation, while the inference of the stated object has already been established. Only the specific varieties have been described, but the definition does not differ.
Therefore, in this context, by means of this effect as a logical mark (*liṅga*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*) also possesses a partial aspect;

hence, the similar example is given because [the sound] arises from an effort for manifestation. That whose existence is inseparable [from its cause], or that which is one's own indivisible nature—[this is what is meant].
The purpose of that classification is so that [the reason] may be non-deviant (avyabhicārī).
It has been stated that those [reasons] such as "conjoined" (saṃyogin) and so forth, for which no such necessary connection (pratibandha) exists,
are not valid reasons, because deviation (vyabhicāra) is possible.
But if there is an obstacle, that very [obstacle] is what establishes the understanding;
for a restriction is indeed inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and that which is non-eternal is not a means of proof.
The exclusivity of the exclusion is called inseparable concomitance.
And that [exclusion] does not exist in things that are not related; for it is precisely from that [relation] that the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) occurs.
Indeed, negative concomitance (*vyatirekitā*) is established only when identity or the state of being a cause has been proven.
Therefore, in the case of a specific [property], there is neither negative concomitance nor positive concomitance.

Having taken up mere non-perception (*adṛṣṭimātra*), only the negative concomitance (*vyatirekitā*) has been stated; therefore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Otherwise, the absence of breath and so forth would be the means of cognition [of selflessness] through its pervasion by selflessness (*nairātmyavyāpti*) upon exclusion.
If it were the case that the vital breaths and so forth would cease upon the cessation of the self, that is not so;
for the cessation of one thing does not logically entail the cessation of another.
If it is argued that they are produced from that [self], this is not the case when the self is perceived.
In that case, when its perception is established, both [perception and non-perception] are established;
however, for something that is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), seeing and not seeing are not established.
Otherwise, how could it be said that [non-perception] does not exist in the case of a jar or similar objects whose form is not seen?
How can there be pervasion of the exclusion [of a property] for one who has not cognized its absence?
Furthermore, the existence or non-existence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth is perceived through their observation in certain instances;
likewise, if the self (*ātman*) were perceptible, its existence or non-existence would be perceived.
If, due to the absence of a certain cause, breath is not observed in a jar,
then it would be logical that its occurrence in the body would also not exist if that cause were absent.
If, on the other hand, the true nature [of the self] were perceived based on some slight similarity even when [the body] is destroyed, [then the analogy would hold].
Since jars and other things are objects of cognition (*prameya*), why is their possession of a self (*sātmatva*) not cognized?
If you say this is undesirable, then indeed valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the basis for all that is desired;
for who else is capable of establishing the distinction between existence and non-existence without it?
Vitality, the closing of the eyes, and so forth, arise from memory, desire, and effort; these [latter] arise from those [former].
Memory, desire, and effort arise from the objects, the senses, and the mind, being produced from their own respective species.
They depend on one another as causes, participating in both positive and negative concomitance.
These two [reasons] exceed the nature of the self (ātmabhāva) when other [infinite] assumptions are made;
they are equivalent to that [reason of audibility] because of the deviation [of the reason] in the case of breath and so forth.
If it is argued that there is no deviation for that [reason] even in the case of negative concomitance (vyatireka), how [can this be]?

Is it not said that its dissociation is from the non-provable alone? In this way, the absence of persistence in the provable follows by implication; that same [dissociation] is equal elsewhere as well.
"Dissociation from the non-provable alone" means that existence in the provable is stated.

For this very reason, it has been stated that by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the perception of two [properties] occurs through one. Therefore, such non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is not established in cases where there is no positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).
Furthermore, what kind of negation could there be other than the negation of a negation, which is itself a form of affirmation?
There is no exclusion of what is non-existent from that which is to be proven; therefore, it does not [apply] to those things that cannot be proven.

If one asks, "Is that very exclusion considered to be the absence of the non-existent?"—the absence of exclusion is indeed an affirmation, the existence of a real entity, even though it pertains to what is non-existent.
But since the non-existence of an entity does not exist, see this as a manifestation of blindness.
If there is no occurrence of the reason with respect to that [non-existence], why is its cessation denied? Even that [cessation] is not a negation; why then is this cessation denied?

Apart from affirmation and negation, there is no other verbal usage; and since that does not exist regarding non-existent things, one would consequently be rendered mute in this regard. Furthermore, there can be no negation of existent things, nor does it apply to non-existent things.
In this world, according to this principle, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) has been brought to dissolution:
if there is a negation of place or time, it is negated as "it exists" [in that location or time];
but it is not negated in the same way that it does not exist [at all].
Therefore, based upon the word and its object— which serve as the basis for both existence and non-existence—
all affirmation and negation here are accepted as having no external foundation.
Through those two, that subject (dharmin) appears as such even in the absence [of an external object].
Because linguistic usage occurs [regarding it], that [non-existence] is also accepted as participating in conventional discourse;
otherwise, in the affirmation and negation of categories of things,
there would be the affirmation and negation of the entire nature of a single property.
Because they do not have different natures, even though there is a distinction [between them], just like affirmation and negation,
there is no coexistence of affirmation and negation in a single substratum (dharmin). With reference to a single substratum that serves as the locus for various properties, [the two are established].
Just as the intellect, when there is an affirmation of one thing, treats other things that possess its characteristics as indifferent,
and when there is a negation, treats those things excluded from it as expectant;
so does it construct a conventional usage whose objects are unreal.
Having approached that very [conceptual construction], which is based on a distinction of objects that are not actually conceptualized,
people do not subvert the worldly object produced by beginningless predispositions.
Therefore, the object— whether it yields its result or does not yield its result— is both distinct and one.
By various disturbances, as if by the depletion of accumulated merit,
even one who does not possess [the object] is brought within the range of vision due to some connection; therefore, those [perceptions] based on distinctions are not understood to be distortions.
And because it functions to establish existence, that [reason] would be doubtful;
for its non-existence is not tenable, since it is accepted [by the opponent] on the basis of a lack of valid cognition.
Furthermore, even if there is no exclusion from what is non-existent, there must still be a turning away from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

The exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is doubtful because of doubt regarding that [exclusion]. When the restriction to one side is established, the exclusion of the other is established.
Even if there is non-perception in the two groups, there may still be doubt regarding those things not perceived.
There are objects that, although not pervading all individuals, arise from that [same] genus;
there is no rule [that they must appear everywhere], just as in the case of being made of earth or being inscribable by iron.
When a contradiction is not observed in their existence, who could remove the doubt?
In some cases, because of restriction [to a specific object], that [self] exists by virtue of being the very nature of its effect; what else could it be?
Even from the absence of self (nairātmya), its exclusion [from such an effect] remains doubtful for that reason.
Let it be so; nevertheless, the self is not established through the absence of self.
Because he does not accept the non-existence of that exclusion (vyatireka) as being a positive entity,
just as [he does not accept] vital breath and so forth as being excluded from the similar instances (sapakṣa) despite their lack of exclusion; therefore,
a reason that lacks exclusion from the similar instances must be one that possesses positive concomitance (anvayin).

If [the reason] possesses positive concomitance (*anvaya*) but lacks negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then there is no absence of self (*anairātmya*) and it is not possessed of a self (*sātmaka*). For that whose own nature is established as being invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) with its activities is alone the negator; therefore, it is also the instigator of activity.

And that invariable concomitance (nāntarīyakatā) depends upon a means of proof; for perception of the effect and non-perception [of it] constitute the causal relation. Indeed, the absence of another entity when that [cause] exists is necessarily its non-cognition.
Because their non-existence is impossible when those [causes] exist,
and because the various effects and specific natures arise from their causes; how could that which arises from something else— which exists without them— possess the nature produced by them?
For the manifold nature of things arises from the diversity of the potencies of their causal complexes;
if that [diversity] were not a differentiator, this world would result in being of a single form.
If there were both differentiation and non-differentiation, the state of having distinct forms would be contradicted.
If a single entity possesses multiple forms, then there would be two forms: that which is fire and that which is other.

If that form which does not produce it [fire] were indeed the same as that [other], then how could that which does not produce it be possible for it? If it is not its form that does not produce it, how could it belong to it?
Therefore, the natures of cause and effect are mutually determined;
consequently, when that [effect] is perceived, it is understood just as if its own nature were being seen.
How can one thing arise from many, as in the case of moisture from milk and water?
Since moisture arises from the power of fluidity (*drava-śakti*), that [power] is indeed one and the same for both.
Is its nature different or non-different? If it is different, how can fluidity be said to be non-different?
It is called "non-different" because the cognition of it is non-distinct in form.

In the same way, even though there is a difference [between individual fires], fire is the basis for the cognition "fire"; by that aspect which does not produce smoke, it is understood as such [i.e., as non-fire]. This is because it arises from a factor of the cognition "fire" itself, while depending on something else.
Smoke does not deviate from that [fire]; thus it is established that the effect is likewise [the means of proof] for another [object].
When fire is present in the locus of smoke, fuel, transformation, and constituent parts, if there were no fire, there would be no smoke; and if there is smoke, there is necessarily fire.
The state of invariable concomitance (nāntarīyakatā) should be understood according to its respective cause,
as was previously explained regarding the nature of destruction and being produced;
this entire logic for understanding the absence of a cause applies to the negative concomitance (vyatireka).
It is to be inferred from the statement of "audibility" being made for the sake of demonstrating parity;

for it is by the exclusion of the reason's own nature that the exclusion of the object is described. Thus, non-perception has been stated as having established examples, but it is not [listed] separately.
In that case as well, because the vital breaths and so forth do not cease upon an imperceptible person,
it is indicated that this [non-apprehension] is a cause of doubt regarding a perceptible object; by this means,
a negation is established that does not admit any portion of a real entity.
However, even regarding real entities, there is an exclusion [of non-existence] by way of affirmation through the two preceding [means of knowledge].
In that regard, for things that are perceptible, existence is nothing other than perception;
thus, the citation of the "one inexpressible" (eka-anupākhyam) is intended to inform the ignorant.

Because the object is non-existent, the subject is negated therein— namely, the cognition, the designation, and the doubt— just as [something] is not fire because it does not burn. Likewise, for other things that are not perceived, there is no existence simply because they are not perceived.
The words for that cognition are established because they are based upon its existence;
for this conventional usage—that "it is non-existent" when it is not perceived despite being perceptible—is already established.
Once that [non-perception] is established, the cognition and the verbal expression regarding its being an effect are also established without doubt.
For when the object is present, one who, out of delusion,
does not state it here is merely reminded of the convention by means of its similarity to what is established,
just as the relationship of cause and effect is proven through perception and non-perception.
For the terms "effect" and so forth have been devised for the sake of conventional usage regarding those two [the cause and the effect].
This establishment of the effect from the cause is included within the essential nature (svabhāva);
thus, an example has been shown separately under the heading of the classification of reasons (hetu).
From the experience of perceiving one thing, there arises the conceptualizing cognition, "I do not perceive this," or "I perceive it"; thus,
the distinction between objects is understood only from a specific perception.
The self-awareness of such [cognitions] is the cause of the cognition of their difference;
therefore, the difference between two cognitions is established by themselves, and from those two, the difference between their objects is established.
Otherwise, due to infinite regress, the difference of anything would not be established.
Because there is an experience of a qualified form, there is no exclusion of anything other than that;
therefore, the perception of that [qualified object] is itself the non-perception of the other.
Thus, this non-perception is established by direct perception itself.
Because its own mere occurrence is the indicator for the establishment of its absence;
otherwise, the non-existence of an object is known through non-perception,
and the non-existence of that perception would have to be known by another, leading to an infinite regress.
Because certainty is impossible regarding that which is unperceivable, its existence elsewhere is precluded;
just as conceptual construction and the like, being without a logical mark (*aliṅga*) among other sentient beings, are not established.
For this [inference] has non-certainty as its result; it is not sufficient for proving exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
The first [type of reason] is employed when the proof is based on certainty alone;
its own form is used in its own applications,
or else its nature as a sublation of the object is used, because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists and does not exist when it is absent.
Alternatively, because their mutual distinction is established— like the certainty of existence and destruction—
or because they are sublated by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)— like the certainty of existence dependent on other factors—
how could there be a restriction [of the effect] when a collection of other causes is present?
If [the cause] exists as the cause of the entity's very existence, what is the point of this laborious succession?
If that cause, having produced another [moment], were the destroyer of that [entity],
then what would happen if it had produced that very same perishable entity?
What could be a benefactor to that [self] which already exists as an established self?
What could be a benefactor to it such that it would have to depend upon it? And how could an entity that is independent ever be otherwise than what it is?
Just as it is not accepted that the very same [entity] which possesses the capacity for non-delay is itself the producer of destruction, [one might argue]:
"If there is no dependence even for a moment, then one entity cannot be the cause of another. If this is said, [we reply]:
For that entity is of such a nature; how could there be an entity in the absence [of its own nature]?
For those things whose existence does not depend on anything else are necessarily existent;
indeed, because of the impossibility of any obstruction, the causal complex is certain in its production of the effect. This [truth] is unfathomable even for one of no small intellectual power.
This teaching of mine, whose supreme essence has not been perceived even through great exertion,
will— finding no worthy recipient in this world—
undergo decay within its own body, like the water of the ocean.
